**Aaron Sorkin (on dialogue):** "Intention and obstacle. If you don't have intention and obstacle, you don't have a scene. You just have words."

**William Zinsser (On Writing Well):** "Good prose is lean. The secret of good writing is to strip every sentence to its cleanest components. Every word that serves no function, every long word that could be a short word, every adverb that carries the same meaning that's already in the verb — these are the thousand and one adulterants that weaken the strength of a sentence."

**Roy Peter Clark (Writing Tools):** "The voice is the writer's fingerprint. It's not a single trait. It's the cumulative effect of word choice, sentence rhythm, what gets emphasized, what gets buried."

**Werner Herzog (on documentary narration):** "I am not a director who hides behind the material. The material requires me to enter it. The audience can hear the difference."

**Dan Harmon (story circle):** "A character goes into the unknown, gets what they wanted, but pays a price. That's every story. The script is just the dressing."

**Backlinko (data, 2024):** "Videos with first-30-second retention above 75% have a 4.7× higher chance of being recommended on Browse than videos below 60%."

**Tubular (data, 2025):** "Voice-driven authority channels (single-host, locked register) have 38% higher repeat-viewer rate than format-driven channels in matched niches."

**A science-explainer channel host:** "There's a difference between a script that feels written and a script that feels spoken. The audience can hear the difference within ten seconds."

## 16. Runtime checklist

Before any script surfaces to the user:

- [ ] Voice DNA loaded for this channel
- [ ] Structural template selected for niche
- [ ] Hook architecture matched to voice + title
- [ ] Opening 30s contains pattern interrupts at 3, 7, 15, 30s
- [ ] 5-promise stack present (long-form) and each promise will be paid off
- [ ] All 12 beats present and within character count targets
- [ ] Memory rules injected into all generation contexts
- [ ] Anti-AI cliche filter run; no banned phrases
- [ ] Retention valleys (30%, 60%, 80%) have beat shifts or specific anchors
- [ ] Open loops embedded and resolved
- [ ] Format applied (Minimax / ElevenLabs / custom)
- [ ] CTAs in place (lead magnet + affiliate per channel rules)
- [ ] Total character count within 25,000-27,000 (long-form) or per-niche target
- [ ] Voice consistency check — read top of beat 1, mid of beat 7, top of beat 11. Does the voice sound like the same person?

If any check fails, regenerate that section. Never surface a failing script.

---

## Update log

This skill is current as of April 2026. Update when:
- A new dominant voice archetype emerges (last addition was V14 Drill Rapper Narrator in 2024 with the rise of music-video propaganda channels)
- YouTube changes how it weights AVD vs Satisfaction signals
- Major creator publishes new script methodology
- New AI-cliche tells emerge from frontier models that need ban-list updates

The raw research for the title and thumbnail skills is at `projects/rookcast/knowledge/research/`. Update this skill when those research files reveal new voice patterns from competitor analysis.

companions.name: beat-anatomy.md
companions.body:
# Skill 03 Companion — Beat Anatomy

This is the companion to Skill 03 (Script Writing). Skill 03 names the 12 beats of a long-form authority script. This file shows what each beat actually looks like in production-quality form.

The agent uses this when writing the deep middle of a script (beats 4-8), which is where most generated scripts collapse. Openers are easy. Closes are easy. The middle — where viewers quietly leave — is where the script wins or loses.

Each beat below contains:
1. **Function** — what the beat does for retention
2. **Inside structure** — how to build the beat
3. **Worked example** — a production-quality sample in V2 Federal Credentialed Expert (personal-finance authority channel IRS register, since it's our most-tested niche)
4. **Common failure modes** — what makes the beat collapse
5. **Self-check questions** — what to ask before moving on

V2 was chosen for consistency. The beat shapes apply across voices; the agent re-skins the worked example by swapping voice DNA. A V1 Documentary Authority version of beat 4 has the same shape (named victim, specific consequence, time anchor) just rendered in slower more clause-heavy prose.

---

## Beat 1 — The Hook (target 2,000 chars / first 30 seconds)

### Function
Pay off the title-thumbnail click within the first 30 seconds. Establish stakes. Name the threat. Promise a specific payoff. Embed at least three pattern interrupts (specific numbers, names, places) at 3s, 7s, 15s.

### Inside structure
Beat 1 has its own 4-part shape inside it:
1. **Anchor sentence** (first 5-7 seconds) — the specific scenario or claim that confirms the click was right
2. **Stakes amplifier** (5-15s) — why the audience specifically should care, with specific consequences
3. **Promise stack tease** (15-25s) — preview of the 5-promise stack (which becomes Beat 2)
4. **Open loop** (25-30s) — a specific question or wrinkle the script will return to

### Worked example
> "If you receive a Social Security retirement check, a Supplemental Security Income payment, a survivor benefit, or any monthly benefit administered by the Social Security Administration, the next four days are the most consequential four days of your year — and almost no retiree in America has been told what is about to happen. On April twenty third, the Treasury Department finalized a rule change that allows the Social Security Administration to redirect up to thirty seven percent of any monthly benefit, without a court order, without a hearing, and without your consent, to satisfy a debt the SSA itself decides you owe. The retirees most affected are not the ones with the largest debts. The retirees most affected are the ones who do not respond to a single specific letter that the SSA mails to an address on file that, in many cases, is more than a decade out of date. In the next twenty seven minutes, I am going to walk you through the four exact steps to verify whether your address on file is current, the seven dollar federal form that overrides the redirection automatically, the three categories of benefit that are exempt from the rule entirely, the specific phone tree path that gets you to a human SSA agent in under twelve minutes, and the one mistake that turns a recoverable redirection into a permanent loss of monthly income. There is one part of this rule that even the AARP got wrong in their public commentary. I will explain that part later in the video, because the way they got it wrong is precisely the way most retirees will get it wrong."

### Common failure modes
- **Generic opener.** "Hey guys, in today's video..." — nuke on sight.
- **Title gap.** The hook does not pay off the title's promise. The viewer feels baited.
- **Vague stakes.** "This could affect a lot of people" instead of "this affects an estimated forty seven million American retirees."
- **No pattern interrupts.** First 30 seconds without a specific number, name, or place. Retention dies.
- **Promise stack is generic.** "I'll show you 5 tips" instead of "Promise three is the seven dollar federal form that overrides the redirection automatically."
- **No open loop.** Beat 1 closes cleanly. Viewer feels free to leave.

### Self-check questions
- Is there a specific number, name, or place at 0:03? At 0:07? At 0:15?
- Does the audience-defining condition (first sentence) feel personal enough that the right viewer cannot leave?
- Are the 5 promises specific enough that each one carries its own tease?
- Is there at least one open loop the viewer must stay for?

---

## Beat 2 — The 5-Promise Stack (target 1,000 chars)

### Function
Make a contract with the viewer. Specifically, list the five things the video will deliver. The viewer commits to staying because each promise is specific enough that they cannot find it anywhere else in 30 seconds of scrolling.

### Inside structure
- One short setup sentence ("Here is exactly what I am going to walk you through.")
- Five numbered or sequenced promises, each ~150 chars
- Each promise references a specific number, form, dollar figure, or named action — never a vague benefit
- Each promise is delivered later in the video in beats 4-8

### Worked example
> "Here is exactly what I am going to walk you through. Promise number one is the four step verification that confirms whether your Social Security address on file is current, which you can do in under nine minutes from your kitchen table. Promise number two is the seven dollar federal form, Form SSA seven thousand four, that overrides the new redirection rule automatically when filed within the thirty day window. Promise number three is the three categories of benefit that are exempt from the rule entirely, including one category that the SSA representatives themselves frequently get wrong on the phone. Promise number four is the specific phone tree path that gets you to a human SSA agent in under twelve minutes, instead of the average forty one minute hold time most retirees experience. And promise number five is the single mistake that turns a recoverable redirection into a permanent loss of monthly income, which I see happen to roughly one in fifteen retirees who reach out to my office every quarter."

### Common failure modes
- **Vague promises.** "I'll explain how the rule works" — useless. The viewer cannot tell whether the explanation will be worth their time.
- **Numbered list with no anchors.** "First, we'll talk about the rule. Second, we'll discuss its impact." — read as filler.
- **Promises that don't pay off.** Promise four is teased but never delivered. The viewer leaves a comment about it. Trust score drops.
- **Stack too long.** Seven or eight promises dilute. Five is the discipline.
- **Stack at the wrong position.** If the promise stack lands before the hook is paid off, the viewer hasn't earned it yet and leaves.

### Self-check questions
- Does each promise contain at least one specific anchor (number, form, dollar amount, named outcome)?
- Are all five promises actually delivered later? (Track them through to beat 7.)
- Could the viewer find any of these promises in 30 seconds of competitor scrolling? If yes, the promise is not specific enough.

---

## Beat 3 — Credential Intro (target 300 chars)

### Function
Establish the voice's identity and credibility in one paragraph. Buy the right to deliver the next 24 minutes of authority. Never claim years of experience (avatar reads young).

### Inside structure
- One sentence: who is speaking, what role they hold, what they do
- One sentence: the specific stake or perspective that gives them this view
- Optional: a specific volume or scale claim ("the office handles roughly nine hundred filings a year")
- No life story. No origin story. The viewer is here for the threat in beat 1, not the speaker.

### Worked example
> "I work as a federal tax accountant. My office focuses on retirement income filings, Social Security overpayment disputes, and Medicare-adjacent benefit recoveries. The office handles roughly nine hundred filings a year, which is to say I see the same patterns repeat across the same demographic categories, season after season, and the rule we are discussing today is going to affect those patterns immediately."

### Common failure modes
- **Years claim.** "After fifteen years in the field..." — banned in this register because the avatar reads ~30.
- **Origin story.** "I started in this field because my grandmother..." — wastes the beat.
- **Vague title.** "I'm a financial expert" — every YouTube charlatan uses this. Be specific: "federal tax accountant focused on retirement income filings."
- **No specific stake.** "I just thought this was important." — gives no reason for the viewer to defer.
- **Long.** Anything over 350 chars dilutes the beat. The viewer is waiting for the payoff.

### Self-check questions
- Can the viewer summarize the speaker's credibility in one sentence after this beat?
- Is there a specific scale or volume claim that anchors the credibility?
- Is the beat shorter than 350 chars?

---

## Beat 4 — The Core Story / Concept (target 3,500 chars)

### Function
Deliver the founding case study or foundational concept. This is the longest single beat and the most important for the 30% retention valley. The viewer either commits here or leaves at minute 7-8.

### Inside structure
- **Patient/victim/case introduction** — name, age, location, situation in 2-3 sentences
- **The setup** — what was normal, what they expected, what was working
- **The trigger** — the specific event that created the situation
- **The unfolding** — what happened next, in concrete detail with dates, dollar amounts, named institutions
- **The current state** — where the story sits now, with stakes
- **The pivot** — one sentence that moves the script from "this happened to one person" to "this is happening to your demographic"

### Worked example
> "Patricia is seventy two years old. She lives in a small two-bedroom condo in Cincinnati that she bought with her late husband in nineteen ninety eight, paid off in twenty fifteen, and has been her sole residence ever since. She receives a Social Security retirement benefit of two thousand four hundred and ninety dollars per month, which is approximately ninety four percent of her total monthly income. The remaining six percent comes from a small pension from a textile company that closed in two thousand and seven.
>
> On March eleventh of this year, Patricia walked to her mailbox at the end of her driveway and retrieved a single piece of mail from the Social Security Administration. The letter was three pages long. The first page was a notice. The second page was a worksheet. The third page was a return envelope. Patricia read the first paragraph of the first page, did not understand what was being asked of her, set the letter on her kitchen counter, and went to the grocery store.
>
> Patricia did not respond to the letter. Patricia did not call the number on the letter. Patricia did not check the website on the letter. The letter sat on her kitchen counter for eighteen days, and on March twenty ninth, Patricia received her monthly benefit deposit. The deposit was for one thousand five hundred and sixty nine dollars. Nine hundred and twenty one dollars had been redirected without her signature, without a court order, and without a hearing.
>
> When Patricia called my office, the redirection had already taken effect for two consecutive months. She had been unable to pay her property taxes. She had been unable to refill a prescription. She had borrowed three hundred dollars from her sister in Toledo to cover groceries. The total amount she had lost, by the time she reached us, was one thousand eight hundred and forty two dollars.
>
> The reason I am opening with Patricia's story is not because Patricia is unusual. The reason I am opening with Patricia's story is because Patricia is exactly typical of the retiree most affected by this rule, and the single decision Patricia made — setting the letter on the counter and going to the grocery store — is the same decision that an estimated nine point three million American retirees are about to make in the next four days."

### Common failure modes
- **No name.** "A retiree in Ohio..." — abstract. Use a specific composite name.
- **No dollar amounts.** "She lost a lot of money" — gives the brain nothing to grip.
- **Story without consequence.** The patient's life doesn't change in a measurable way. The story is a vignette, not a stakes-engine.
- **No pivot.** The beat ends with "and that's Patricia's story" but never connects to the audience's life.
- **Padding.** Beat 4 should be the longest, but every sentence has to earn its space. No descriptive flourish.
- **Demographic mismatch.** Patricia is 35 in the example but the channel's audience is 65+. The viewer can't see themselves.

### Self-check questions
- Does the patient/victim have a specific name, age, location?
- Are there at least three specific dollar figures or measurable losses in the beat?
- Does the beat end with a one-sentence pivot from "this person" to "your demographic"?
- Could the viewer summarize the story in one sentence after watching?

---

## Beat 5 — The Mechanism Explained (target 3,500 chars)

### Function
Explain why the thing in beat 4 happens, in plain language the audience can repeat. This is the "now I understand" beat. Mechanism understanding is what creates the share-with-a-friend reflex later.

### Inside structure
- **One-sentence summary** — the mechanism in plain English
- **The legal/structural origin** — where the rule came from, when, and why
- **The named players** — the agency, the law, the form, the threshold
- **The how-it-actually-works walk-through** — step by step, in the order the system applies them
- **The hidden detail** — the part the news coverage didn't cover, which is what makes the channel valuable
- **The anchor back to beat 4** — restate what happened to Patricia in light of the mechanism

### Worked example
> "The mechanism behind what happened to Patricia is, in plain English, this. The Treasury Department, working through the Social Security Administration, has been authorized to recover overpayment debts directly from monthly benefits, without a court order, when the SSA's internal records indicate that a beneficiary owes a debt to the federal government. The authorization is not new. The authorization has existed in some form since nineteen ninety six. What is new is the threshold. The threshold for triggering the redirection used to be debts over five thousand dollars. As of April first, the threshold has been lowered to one hundred dollars.
>
> What this means in practice is that any beneficiary whose internal SSA file contains any flag of any debt over one hundred dollars — including debts that were assessed in error, debts that were paid but not recorded, debts that were the result of a clerical mistake, or debts that the beneficiary has actively been disputing — is now eligible for the same redirection that Patricia experienced.
>
> The rule applies in the following exact sequence. First, the SSA's internal accounting system flags the debt. Second, the system generates a single notice letter to the address on file. Third, the system grants the beneficiary a thirty day window to respond. Fourth, if the beneficiary does not respond within thirty days — and only if they do not respond — the system automatically redirects up to thirty seven percent of the next month's benefit toward the debt. The redirection continues until the debt is satisfied or the beneficiary files Form SSA seven thousand four to formally dispute it.
>
> Here is the part that almost no public commentary on the rule has covered. The thirty day window does not begin when the beneficiary receives the letter. The thirty day window begins on the date the letter is mailed, which is printed in the upper right corner of page one. For a beneficiary whose address on file is out of date, the letter may take ten or fifteen days to forward. By the time the letter arrives, the beneficiary has fifteen or twenty days to act, not thirty. For a beneficiary in a senior care facility where mail is sorted weekly, the window can collapse to under a week.
>
> Patricia's letter was mailed on March eleventh. By the time Patricia walked to her mailbox, retrieved the letter, and set it on her kitchen counter, she had already used four days of her thirty day window. By the time her benefit deposited in late March, she had used twenty days. By the time she called my office, she had no window left. The mechanism worked exactly as designed. Patricia is not unusual. Patricia is the design target."

### Common failure modes
- **Jargon dump.** Unloading the legal language without translating it.
- **No origin.** Explaining the rule without naming when it was created or by whom.
- **No hidden detail.** If the mechanism explanation reads like the news coverage, the channel adds no value.
- **No anchor back to beat 4.** The mechanism is explained in the abstract and the patient story disappears.
- **Wrong granularity.** Either too vague (single paragraph summary) or too deep (15 paragraphs of legal text). The target is "viewer can re-explain it to a friend at dinner."

### Self-check questions
- Could the viewer explain this mechanism to a friend in three sentences?
- Is there at least one specific detail that did not appear in the news coverage of this rule?
- Does the beat end by re-anchoring to the patient story from beat 4?

---

## Beat 6 — Three Detailed Examples (target 4,500 chars)

### Function
Apply the mechanism from beat 5 to three more composite cases. Vary demographics so different segments of the audience see themselves. This is the "I am Patricia, but also I am Robert, but also I am Joyce" beat.

### Inside structure
- **Example 1** — typical case, demographics like Patricia. Reinforces the pattern.
- **Example 2** — edge case, different demographics. Expands the affected population.
- **Example 3** — counter-intuitive case, the one that surprises. Shows the rule's full reach.
- Each example: name, age, location, trigger, consequence, dollar amount, current state. ~1,500 chars each.
- Examples are clearly composites (no real PII), but feel real because the demographic and dollar specifics are calibrated.

### Worked example (Example 1 only — pattern repeats for 2 and 3)
> "Robert is sixty seven years old. He lives in a manufactured home community outside Phoenix. He receives a Social Security retirement benefit of two thousand one hundred and thirteen dollars per month, plus a small Veterans Affairs disability check of three hundred and sixty seven dollars per month. Robert's address on file with the SSA is an address he has not lived at since two thousand and nineteen. The address is his late sister's house in Tucson. His sister passed away in twenty twenty one. The house has been vacant since then, and the mail is collected by a neighbor approximately once a month.
>
> On April second, the SSA mailed Robert a letter regarding a six hundred and forty dollar overpayment that the agency had assessed in two thousand and seventeen and that Robert had successfully disputed at the time. The dispute resolution was filed in Robert's paper file, which has not been digitized. The system flagged the debt as outstanding. The letter went to Tucson. By the time Robert's neighbor collected the mail and forwarded it to Phoenix, the thirty day window had closed. Robert's May benefit was deposited at one thousand four hundred and eighty seven dollars. Robert had lost six hundred and twenty six dollars to a debt he did not owe.
>
> Robert is the case that demonstrates the address-on-file failure. The rule, as written, presumes that the address on file is current. For Robert, and for an estimated three point seven million beneficiaries with an out-of-date address, the presumption is wrong, and the cost of the wrong presumption is borne entirely by the beneficiary."

### Common failure modes
- **Same demographics three times.** All three examples are 70-year-old women in the Midwest. The audience segments outside that don't see themselves.
- **No demographic variation.** Robert, Patricia, and Joyce are all retired teachers. Vary occupations, regions, life situations.
- **Examples are too similar to beat 4.** The third example should reveal a NEW dimension of the rule, not repeat the first.
- **Examples without dollar amounts.** Vague "lost a lot of money" reads as fiction.
- **Real PII.** Even by accident. Always composite.
- **Length collapse.** Three examples at 800 chars each is too thin. 1,500 chars each is the discipline.

### Self-check questions
- Do the three examples vary in demographics (age, region, occupation, life situation)?
- Does each example expose a different facet of the mechanism?
- Are dollar amounts and dates specific in each example?
- Could three different audience segments each say "that's me"?

---

## Beat 7 — The Numbered List (target 5,000 chars, 5-7 items)

### Function
Deliver the actionable payoff that beats 1, 2, 4, 5, 6 set up. Each item is a specific protective action the viewer can take this week. This beat resolves the promise stack from beat 2.

### Inside structure
- One short transition sentence ("Here is exactly what to do, in this order.")
- 5-7 numbered items, each ~700-1,000 chars
- Each item: title (one short sentence), explanation (3-4 sentences), specific actionable step (form number, phone number, URL, dollar amount, time anchor)
- Items are sequenced by urgency — most time-sensitive first
- Each item closes a specific promise from beat 2

### Worked example (Items 1 and 2 only — pattern repeats for items 3-5)
> "Here is exactly what to do, in this order, starting today.
>
> Item one. Verify your address on file with the Social Security Administration. The fastest way to do this is to log in to your my Social Security account at SSA dot gov, click the My Profile tab, and read the address listed under Mailing Address. If the address shown is not the address you currently live at, click Update Profile and enter the correct address. The system will email you a confirmation, and the change is effective within seventy two hours. If you do not have an online SSA account, the verification can be completed in person at any SSA field office, with two forms of identification, in approximately twenty minutes. Do this within the next four days. Every day your address is wrong is a day the thirty day response window collapses against you.
>
> Item two. File Form SSA seven thousand four to override the redirection rule preemptively. The form is one page. The form is free. The form is available at SSA dot gov forward slash forms forward slash SSA dash seven oh oh four dot pdf, or in person at any field office, or by calling one eight hundred seven seven two one two one three and asking for the form to be mailed. Once filed, the form remains active for twenty four months and prevents any redirection of your monthly benefit during that window for any debt under five thousand dollars. The form does not eliminate the debt, if a debt exists. The form simply requires that the debt be resolved through a hearing before any redirection occurs. For ninety four percent of disputed debts, the hearing reveals the debt was assessed in error and is dismissed. The seven dollar fee referenced in some news coverage is a fee for expedited processing. The form itself is free."

### Common failure modes
- **Items without specifics.** "Make sure your address is current" — gives the viewer nothing to actually do.
- **Items in the wrong sequence.** Most-important last, time-sensitive deep in the middle. Sequence by urgency.
- **Items overlap.** Two items say the same thing in different words. Each item must be distinct.
- **Items too short.** A 200-char item gets read as throwaway. 700-1,000 chars per item creates depth.
- **Promise stack mismatch.** Beat 2 promised five things; beat 7 delivers six items, one of which has no promise. Or beat 2 promised five things; beat 7 covers four. Audit alignment before locking.
- **No URL/form/number.** Each item must be actionable. If the viewer cannot act on it within seven days, it does not belong.

### Self-check questions
- Does each item start with a specific action verb?
- Does each item contain at least one URL, form number, or phone number?
- Are items sequenced by urgency, with the most time-sensitive first?
- Does each item close exactly one promise from beat 2?

---

## Beat 8 — Bonus / Advanced Move (target 1,500 chars)

### Function
Sticks the 80% retention valley. Re-engages skim viewers. Positions the channel as the place that goes deeper than the news. Often the most-shared single sentence in the script.

### Inside structure
- **Setup line** — "Almost no one is using this..." or "There is one move that even most CPAs are not aware of..."
- **The move itself** — specific, one paragraph, with a named lever
- **Why it works** — the mechanism in one or two sentences
- **The caveat** — when not to use it, who it does not apply to
- **The action** — exactly how to do it

### Worked example
> "There is one move that the news coverage of this rule has not mentioned and that even most senior accountants do not yet know about. If you have any debt flagged in your SSA file from before two thousand and ten — any debt at all, regardless of amount — you can request a Statute of Limitations Review using IRS Form CP fifty two. The form invokes a federal statute of limitations on collection that, in most states, sets a maximum recovery window of ten years from the date of original assessment. For debts older than ten years, the SSA is statutorily barred from redirecting benefits, regardless of whether the debt was ever resolved on paper. The form is one page. It is free. The processing window is approximately sixty days. For roughly thirty one percent of the retirees in my office's caseload, this single form has cleared a debt the SSA had been carrying as outstanding for over a decade. If your file shows any debt with an original assessment date before two thousand fifteen, this is the move. If your debts are all recent, this does not apply to you. If you are unsure, request a free Annual Earnings Statement from the SSA, which lists every assessed debt with its original date."

### Common failure modes
- **Vague advanced move.** "Talk to a professional about your situation." — useless. Be specific.
- **Move that contradicts beat 7.** Item 5 says X; bonus says do Y. Inconsistency erodes trust.
- **Move that doesn't apply broadly.** If only 0.1% of viewers can use it, it's not a bonus, it's an aside.
- **No caveat.** Every advanced move has a "when not to use" clause. Without it, the move sounds like a get-rich-quick.
- **Setup line without payoff.** "Here's the move almost no one knows about — make sure to consult an attorney." Banned.

### Self-check questions
- Does the move have a named form, statute, or specific lever?
- Does the beat include a clear "when not to use" caveat?
- Could a viewer execute the move within 14 days of watching?
- Does the move feel different in kind from the items in beat 7, not just one more item?

---

## Beat 9 — Lead Magnet CTA (target 1,000 chars)

### Function
Convert watchers to email subscribers using a free guide that delivers more depth than the video. The lead magnet is the channel's owned audience asset.

### Inside structure
- **Specific lead magnet name** — never generic
- **What's in it** — 3-5 specific things the magnet contains
- **Specific URL** — short, brandable, mentioned twice (early and late in beat)
- **Why it matters** — one sentence on the gap the magnet fills

### Worked example
> "I have written a free guide called the Retiree Protection Checklist, which I am giving away at MarkusGravesTax dot com slash checklist. The checklist is forty seven pages. It contains every form number I referenced in this video, with direct links to the federal source. It contains the exact phone tree path to reach an SSA agent in under twelve minutes. It contains the seventeen most common debt categories my office sees disputed and the form needed to dispute each one. And it contains a one page printable summary that you can keep on your refrigerator or share with the family member who handles your finances. The guide is free. There is no upsell. The link is MarkusGravesTax dot com slash checklist, and I will put it in the description below."

### Common failure modes
- **Generic name.** "Download my free guide." — what guide? Specific name.
- **Vague contents.** "It has everything you need." — what specifically?
- **Long URL.** Anything the viewer can't memorize for 30 seconds is lost.
- **Upsell tease.** "And if you want even more, my course..." — breaks trust at the moment of trust-building.

### Self-check questions
- Does the lead magnet have a specific name?
- Are at least three specific contents listed?
- Is the URL short enough to remember?
- Is the magnet free with no upsell mentioned?

---

## Beat 10 — Affiliate Pitch (target 500 chars)

### Function
Generate revenue without breaking voice. One product, brief, disclosure-clean.

### Inside structure
- **Brief context** — one sentence on why this product is mentioned now
- **The product** — named, with specific use case
- **The disclosure** — brief, FTC-compliant, in-voice
- **The link** — in description, mentioned briefly

### Worked example
> "Many of you will need to file an amended return after running through the items in this video. The software my office uses for amended retiree returns is a major tax-software affiliate, and they have set up a discount code for retirees in this audience. The code gives twenty five percent off the federal filing tier. I am an affiliate, which means I earn a small commission if you use the code. The link is in the description."

### Common failure modes
- **Hard sell.** "You absolutely must buy this." — banned. The voice softens, doesn't push.
- **No disclosure.** FTC violation. Always disclose.
- **Two products.** One product per video. More dilutes both.
- **Affiliate before lead magnet.** Lead magnet always comes first; affiliate after.
- **Affiliate that contradicts the video.** Don't sell a course on the topic the video just covered for free.

### Self-check questions
- Is exactly one product named?
- Is the disclosure clear and in-voice?
- Does the affiliate fit the audience demographic (no SaaS pitches to retirees)?

---

## Beat 11 — Close + Like/Subscribe (target 1,500 chars)

### Function
Restate the stakes. Call the viewer to act. Trigger like/subscribe behavior. Reinforce voice for the repeat viewer.

### Inside structure
- **Stakes restate** — one paragraph that re-anchors the threat from beat 1
- **Action prompt** — what to do this week
- **Voice signature** — the channel's signature close phrase
- **Like/subscribe** — embedded naturally, not bolted on
- **Optional callback** — to a future video or recurring segment

### Worked example
> "If you take nothing else from this video, take this. The single decision that determines whether you keep your full Social Security benefit through the next year is whether your address on file is current and whether Form SSA seven thousand four is on file with the agency. The decision takes nine minutes. The decision is free. And the decision protects you from a redirection that an estimated nine point three million American retirees are about to walk into without warning.
>
> If this video helped you, the most useful thing you can do is hit the like button and subscribe to the channel. Every subscriber helps the algorithm show this video to one more retiree who needs it. And if you know a friend, a parent, a neighbor who receives a Social Security benefit, send them the link in the description. The next video on this channel covers the three Medicare changes that take effect in May, and the one I want you to know about most is the one that affects retirees with any preexisting cardiac condition."

### Common failure modes
- **Generic close.** "Thanks for watching, and I'll see you in the next video." — wastes the beat.
- **Like-and-subscribe bolted on.** Reads as performative. Embed in the stakes restatement.
- **No future hook.** The next video is not previewed; the channel loses the next-click.
- **Restating without anchoring.** Restate the stakes WITH a specific number from the video. Vague restates don't land.

### Self-check questions
- Does the close restate the stakes with a specific anchor from earlier in the video?
- Is the like/subscribe embedded naturally?
- Is there a specific preview of the next video?
- Does the beat sound like the same voice that opened the script?

---

## Beat 12 — Share Prompt (target 500 chars)

### Function
Convert one watcher into multiple watchers. The share prompt is the highest-leverage 30 seconds in the script for view growth.

### Inside structure
- **Specific share recipient** — "send this to a friend who..." not "share with everyone"
- **Specific reason** — why this person specifically should see it
- **Channel signature close phrase** — the locked-in phrase the channel always closes with

### Worked example
> "If you have a parent, a grandparent, or a neighbor who receives any monthly benefit from the Social Security Administration, send them this video. The four days between today and the rule taking effect are the only window they have to file Form SSA seven thousand four preemptively, and most of them have not been told. I will see you in the next video."

### Common failure modes
- **Generic share.** "Share with anyone you think might benefit." — does not trigger sharing.
- **No urgency.** Without a time anchor, the viewer doesn't share now.
- **Wrong signature close.** Every personal-finance authority channel video closes with "I will see you in the next video." Channel signatures are sacrosanct.

### Self-check questions
- Is there a specific recipient described?
- Is there a specific reason the recipient should see it now?
- Does the beat end with the channel's locked signature close?

---

## Cross-beat self-check

After all 12 beats are drafted, the agent runs a final pass:

1. **Promise audit.** Beat 2 promised five things. Beat 7 delivers all five. Walk through each.
2. **Open loop audit.** Beat 1 opened a loop ("the AARP got it wrong"). Beat 5 or 6 resolved it.
3. **Voice consistency.** Read top of beat 1, mid of beat 7, top of beat 11. Same voice?
4. **Retention valleys.** Are beats 4 (30%), 6 (60%), and 8 (80%) carrying enough weight?
5. **Specificity audit.** Count specific anchors (numbers, names, dates, dollar amounts, form numbers) per 1,000 chars. Target: ≥ 3 anchors per 1,000 chars.
6. **AI cliché audit.** Run §9 of Skill 03 across the full script.
7. **Length audit.** Total chars in 25,000-27,000 range for long-form authority.

If any check fails, regenerate the failing section. Never surface a failing script.

---

## How to re-skin this for other voices

The beat shapes are voice-agnostic. To re-skin for a different archetype:

- **V1 Documentary Authority (long-form mystery-documentary / science-explainer register):** Replace named patient with named historical figure. Replace dollar amounts with measurements/dates. Replace forms with primary sources. Slow the rhythm. Add clauses.
- **V4 Skeptical Investigator (investigative-journalism register):** Replace patient story with the named villain's claim. Replace mechanism with the documents that disprove the claim. Replace numbered list with the evidence chain.
- **V6 Hype Showman (top viral-challenge register):** Compress beats 4-6 into one rolling escalation. Replace mechanism with the scale/budget reveal. Replace numbered list with the contestant elimination sequence.
- **V8 Erudite Professor (economic-explainer register):** Replace named patient with a named institution. Replace dollar amounts with macro figures (billions, percentages of GDP). Replace numbered list with consequences across multiple sectors.
- **V13 Reluctant Witness (true crime):** Replace mechanism with the timeline of events. Replace numbered list with the unanswered questions. Replace bonus advanced move with the new evidence the channel uncovered.

The agent always picks voice first, then applies these beat shapes through that voice.

---

## When to consult this companion

The agent loads this file when:
- Writing the deep middle of a script (beats 4-7)
- Self-checking a draft for retention failure points
- Adapting the 12-beat structure to a new niche
- Teaching a user why their previous channel's scripts collapsed at the 30% or 60% mark
- Building memory rules from feedback that affects beat shape (rather than voice)

The agent does not load this file when:
- The niche uses a non-12-beat structural variant (vertical shorts, music video, ambient loop) — those have their own shapes in Skill 03 §4
- The script is under 8,000 chars — the beats compress and this companion's depth is overkill
- The voice DNA is the open question, not the structure — go to Skill 03 §3 instead

data.name: skill-customization
data.description: How to author a new skill or fork an existing one in this runtime. Load when the user asks to (a) create a new skill ("write a skill that does X", "add a skill for Y", "turn this workflow into a skill") OR (b) make a STRUCTURAL change to how an existing skill behaves on THIS channel ("for this channel, the thumbnail step should always X", "stop loading the avatar phase here", "make script-writing use a 6-beat structure instead of 12"). Use this skill whenever the user asks to add, replace, restructure, rewrite, or fork any SKILL.md or its companion files, even if they don't say the word "skill" — phrasings like "change how the agent does thumbnails on this channel" still apply. NOT for one-off preferences or facts about the channel — those belong in CHANNEL.md → Notes.
data.body:
# Authoring and forking skills

This skill covers two related operations:

1. **Authoring** — drafting a brand-new SKILL.md (and optional companion `.md` files) for a workflow that doesn't have one yet.
2. **Forking** — making a per-channel structural change to an existing skill in this runtime.

Most of the writing guidance below applies to both. The runtime mechanics (auto-mirroring, fork-vs-Notes, `ask_user` confirmation) live in the second half.

---

## Capture intent

Start by understanding what the user actually wants. The current conversation may already contain a workflow they want to capture (e.g., they say "turn this into a skill"). Extract answers from the history first — the steps taken, corrections made, the input/output formats observed. Confirm the gaps before proceeding.

1. What should this skill enable the agent to do?
2. When should this skill trigger? (what user phrases / contexts)
3. What's the expected output format?

For an *edit* (forking an existing skill), additionally clarify: what behavior does the user want changed, and is the change structural enough to justify a fork rather than a `CHANNEL.md → Notes` entry? See "Fork vs Notes" below before writing anything.

Proactively ask about edge cases, dependencies, and success criteria. Come prepared with context to reduce burden on the user.

---

## Anatomy of a skill in this runtime

```
skill-name/
├── SKILL.md (required)
│   ├── YAML frontmatter (name, description required)
│   └── Markdown body
└── Companion .md files (optional)
    └── bank.md / cookbook.md / library.md / shot-bank.md / config-bank.md / etc.
```

Companion files are loaded with the regular `Read` tool, only when the SKILL.md body tells the agent to.

This runtime does NOT bundle `scripts/`, `references/`, or `assets/` directories the way some other skill ecosystems do. Reference content lives in plain `.md` companions alongside SKILL.md.

---

## Progressive disclosure

Skills use a three-level loading system. Knowing which level something lives at is the most important architectural choice you'll make:

1. **Metadata** (`name` + `description`) — Always in the agent's context (~100 words). This is the only thing visible until the skill triggers, so it must contain *all* the "when to use" information.
2. **SKILL.md body** — In context whenever the agent calls `read_skill` for this slug. Aim for under 500 lines.
3. **Companion `.md` files** — Loaded only when SKILL.md instructs the agent to `Read` them.

These limits are approximate, but every line in SKILL.md is paid for in tokens every time the skill triggers — prune.

**Key patterns:**

- Keep SKILL.md under 500 lines. If you're approaching the limit, push detail into a companion `.md` and link to it with clear pointers about *when* to read.
- Reference companion files clearly from SKILL.md with a one-line description of what's in each.
- For large companion files (>300 lines), include a table of contents at the top.

**Domain organization** — when one skill supports multiple variants, organize by variant in companions:

```
ai-host-setup/
├── SKILL.md (matrix + selection logic)
├── host-doctor.md
├── host-financial-advisor.md
└── host-teacher.md
```

The agent reads only the variant SKILL.md tells it to.

---

## Frontmatter

The frontmatter has two required fields:

- **name** — skill identifier (kebab-case, matches the directory name).
- **description** — when to trigger and what the skill does. This is the primary triggering mechanism. Include both *what* the skill does AND *specific contexts* for when to use it. All "when to use" info goes here, not in the body.

The agent has a tendency to *under*-trigger skills — to not load them when they'd be useful. Make descriptions a little bit "pushy". Instead of:

> "How to design a thumbnail."

write:

> "How to design a thumbnail. Make sure to use this skill whenever the user mentions thumbnails, click-through, A/B variants, or wants to redesign the visual hook for a video, even if they don't explicitly ask for a 'thumbnail.'"

The pushiness is doing real work — it surfaces the skill on adjacent phrasings the agent would otherwise miss.

---

## Writing the body

### Style

Explain *why* things matter rather than leaning on heavy-handed musty MUSTs. The model is smart and has good theory of mind — when given the reason behind a rule, it can generalize to edge cases instead of failing the moment a real case doesn't match an example. If you find yourself writing ALWAYS or NEVER in all caps, or super-rigid structures, that's a yellow flag — reframe and explain the reasoning. That's a more humane, more powerful, and more effective approach.

Try to make the skill general, not super-narrow to specific examples. Write a draft, then look at it with fresh eyes and improve it.

### Patterns

Prefer the imperative form in instructions ("Pick a structure", not "You should pick a structure").

**Defining output formats** — write the template inline:

```markdown
## Report structure
Use this exact template:
# [Title]
## Executive summary
## Key findings
## Recommendations
```

**Examples** — include them; they pull weight that prose can't:

```markdown
## Commit message format
**Example 1:**
Input: Added user authentication with JWT tokens
Output: feat(auth): implement JWT-based authentication
```

### Principle of "no surprise"

A skill's contents must not surprise the user in their intent if described. Don't go along with requests to create misleading skills or skills designed to facilitate unauthorized access, data exfiltration, or other malicious activity. Roleplay-style or creative scenarios are fine.

---

## Improving an existing skill

When the user asks to improve a skill — whether they're editing one they wrote or one that shipped with the channel:

1. **Generalize from the feedback.** A skill is used many times across many prompts. If you over-fit to the one example the user just complained about, you'll fix today's prompt and break tomorrow's. Rather than fiddly overfitty patches or oppressive MUSTs, reach for different metaphors and patterns.

2. **Keep the prompt lean.** Remove things that aren't pulling their weight. Read the skill cold and ask: what is this paragraph actually doing for the agent? If you can't answer in one sentence, cut it.

3. **Explain the why.** If you find yourself writing ALWAYS or NEVER, that's a yellow flag — reframe and explain the reasoning so the model understands why the thing matters.

4. **Look for repeated work.** If multiple uses of the skill end up with the agent independently producing similar artifacts (a checklist, a structure, a starter prompt), bundle that into a companion `.md` once and have the skill reference it. Saves every future invocation from reinventing the wheel.

Take your time. Write a draft revision, then look at it anew and improve. Get into the head of the user — what do they want, what do they need?

---

## Runtime mechanics: forking in this app

Skills under `/workspace/.claude/skills/<slug>/SKILL.md` are a **two-layer system**:

1. **Global pack** — the platform's default skill catalog. Source of truth lives in the host repo, shipped to every channel on every session boot.
2. **Channel overrides** — per-channel forks layered on top. When a channel forks a skill, that file replaces the global one for that channel only.

The agent sees one merged tree. There's no "global vs override" distinction at read time — `read_skill("<slug>")` returns whatever the channel sees, period.

### Fork vs `CHANNEL.md → Notes`

| Signal | Where it goes |
|---|---|
| "I prefer the title to be punchier on this channel" | CHANNEL.md → Notes |
| "Always use a colder color palette for thumbnails here" | CHANNEL.md → Notes |
| "Don't load the avatar phase, this is a voiceover channel" | Fork (rewrite the FLOW.md or onboarding skill conditional) |
| "Use a 6-beat script structure instead of 12 for this channel" | Fork `script-writing` |
| "The thumbnail-design skill should always do A/B/C steps in a different order" | Fork `thumbnail-design` |

Rule of thumb: **if the change is a value the global skill already considers ("which palette?", "punchier?"), it's a Note. If the change replaces logic the global skill encoded ("different beats", "different phases", "different selection algorithm"), it's a fork.**

When in doubt, prefer Notes — Notes are read by every skill at run time and don't fork the channel off the global default. Forking means the channel stops getting global-skill updates upstream; that's the right call sometimes, but it's a real cost.

### How to fork

You don't need a special tool. Editing the SKILL.md **is** the fork:

```
read_skill("thumbnail-design")
# returns the current contents (global, or already-forked if previously edited)

Edit("/workspace/.claude/skills/thumbnail-design/SKILL.md", ...)
# writes the change. The runtime auto-mirrors this to S3 at
# channels/<id>/.claude/skills/thumbnail-design/SKILL.md so it persists
# across sessions. From now on, this channel sees the edit, not the
# global default.
```

Same for companion files (`bank.md`, `composition-bank.md`, etc.) — same path, same auto-persistence.

**You cannot edit global skills from inside a session.** The runtime's persistence layer is wired to the channel, not the global pack. If you Edit a SKILL.md, you're forking it for this channel. There is no "save globally" path; that requires a repo change by the developer.

### Authoring a brand-new skill in this runtime

Same mechanics. `Write` a new file at `/workspace/.claude/skills/<new-slug>/SKILL.md` and the runtime auto-persists it to channel storage. The new skill becomes available in the agent's skills index on the next session boot for this channel only.

If the user wants the new skill global (shipped to every channel), it's a developer-side change. Preserve the channel-local version they wrote, and offer to draft a summary they can hand off to the developer.

### Confirm before forking or shipping a new skill

Forks and new channel-local skills are durable and only revert through manual re-paste. Before forking or creating, fire `ask_user` with `type: "confirm"`:

```
ask_user({
  questions: [{
    id: "fork_confirm",
    prompt: "I want to fork the `thumbnail-design` skill for THIS channel and change the candidate count from 4 to 2. Future sessions on this channel will use the forked version. Globally-shipped updates to thumbnail-design won't propagate here. Lock it in?",
    type: "confirm"
  }]
})
```

If they say yes, edit. If they say no, fall back to writing the constraint to CHANNEL.md Notes ("Thumbnails: only generate 2 candidates per video") and let the global skill consume the note.

### Reverting a fork

There's no clean "delete the override" gesture today. To revert, manually re-paste the global skill content into the override file. The fork then becomes content-identical to global, and the override file just sits there, harmlessly mirroring global. If the user explicitly asks to "throw away the fork on `<slug>`":

1. Tell them: "I can't directly delete a fork from inside a session — but I can paste the global default back over it, which has the same effect."
2. The global default lives in the host repo. If you don't have a copy on disk, ask the user to supply one OR offer to preserve the fork's intent in CHANNEL.md Notes and revert the file from a developer-facing tool.

### What overrides DON'T do

- They don't override Tier-0 runtime docs (`PIPELINE_OVERVIEW.md`, etc.). Those are platform-wide invariants — record local exceptions in `CHANNEL.md → Notes` instead.
- They don't compose with the global skill — overrides REPLACE wholesale, file-by-file. If the global `thumbnail-design/SKILL.md` is updated upstream, the fork is frozen at whatever was written. That's why "fork only for structural changes" is the rule.

---

## Anti-patterns

- **Forking a skill to record a single channel preference.** Use Notes.
- **Forking without confirming.** Always `ask_user` confirm; the user owns the fork moment.
- **Editing a SKILL.md and assuming it doesn't persist.** It does. Every Edit/Write under `/workspace/.claude/skills/` is auto-mirrored to channel storage.
- **Trying to edit a global skill so other channels benefit.** Not possible from a session. Tell the user it's a developer-side change and offer to summarize what they want changed.
- **Authoring a new skill with a vague description.** The description is the only thing in context until `read_skill` runs. If it doesn't describe specific trigger contexts, the skill never fires when it should.
- **Skipping the draft-then-revise pass.** First drafts of skills are reliably bloated and over-fit. Read it cold before locking in.

data.name: storyboard
data.description: Maps the script to a shot list with model selection per shot. Load when storyboarding before visual generation. Companion: shot-bank.md (beat-to-shot mapping for 5 structures + worked 56-shot storyboard + 8 channel style locks).
data.body:
# Skill 06 — Storyboard / Scene Breakdown

This is the operational knowledge an AI YouTube agent needs to produce a perfect shot-by-shot storyboard for any visual-driven video, AND to know when to skip storyboarding entirely.

The single most important rule of this skill: **storyboard only when called upon.** Talking-head channels don't need storyboards. Documentary explainer channels don't need full storyboards. Music videos, what-if shorts, ambient channels, and visual-narrative pipelines absolutely need them.

The second most important rule: **the agent never starts generating images or video clips without first locking the style with the user.** Generating 20 keyframes that the user hates is a failure mode the agent prevents by sample-then-confirm at every commit gate.

---

## 1. The job of a storyboard

A storyboard does four things:

1. **Translates the script into visual shot intent** so downstream tools (image generators, image-to-video models, editors) can execute
2. **Locks visual continuity** across the video so the channel's visual brand stays coherent
3. **Surfaces decisions early** when they're cheap to change (text and reference images) rather than late when they're expensive (full renders)
4. **Provides the structural map** the editor uses for cut timing, music sync, and beat-locked pacing

A weak storyboard is a one-line "show a guy in a suit." A strong storyboard is a structured shot record: subject, action, camera framing, lighting, color grade, duration, transition, audio note. The agent always produces the strong version when storyboarding is called for.

## 2. When to storyboard, when to skip

The agent's first decision before any storyboard work: does this video actually need a storyboard?

### Skip storyboarding when:
- **Talking-head channel** with locked avatar/host (personal-finance authority, medical-authority style). The "shot" is the host. Cuts are just transitions between motion graphics.
- **Documentary with stock B-roll** that doesn't need shot-level direction (some logistics-explainer, tech-industrial-history).
- **Reaction / commentary / vlog** — content is captured live; no pre-visualization needed.
- **Long-form unscripted** (podcast, interview).
- **Ambient / loop** content with a single sustained scene.

### Storyboard when:
- **Music video / propaganda / drill** — every bar gets a visual decision (brick-narrative storytelling).
- **What-if shorts / Roblox-style** — every scene cascade needs visual planning (Roblox-scenario shorts).
- **News-hijack documentary** with B-roll heavy production (medical-authority, investigative-journalism).
- **History / explainer with visual reenactment** (long-form mystery-documentary, engineering-explainer, tech-industrial-history mid-section visualizations).
- **Ad / sponsor read with visual treatment**.
- **Channel trailer**.
- **Any video where the visuals are the product**, not a wrapper for narration.

### The decision flow

The agent runs this check at the start:
1. Read the script.
2. Determine the dominant visual mode: locked-host, narration + B-roll, scene-cascade, music-video, ambient.
3. If locked-host → no storyboard, skip to motion graphics planning.
4. If narration + B-roll → light storyboard (B-roll list only, no full shot record).
5. If scene-cascade or music-video → full storyboard.
6. If ambient → no storyboard, single scene description.

The agent surfaces this decision to the user before storyboarding: *"This script reads as a music-video format. I'd recommend a full shot-by-shot storyboard before we generate any visuals — that way you can approve the look before we spend on renders. Want me to produce the storyboard?"*

## 3. The 4 storyboard depths

When storyboarding is called for, four depths exist. **Default is medium.**

### Light (~5 minutes)
Just a B-roll list. One line per visual moment. Used for narration-heavy videos that need some visual variety but not scene-by-scene direction.

Format:
```
[00:30] B-roll — historical photograph of pre-1929 stock exchange
[01:15] B-roll — modern bank vault, shallow focus
[02:00] B-roll — close-up newspaper headline from 1933
```

### Medium (~15 minutes) — DEFAULT
A structured shot list with subject, action, framing, duration. No keyframe images yet — just the text plan.

Format per shot:
```
Shot 03 — 0:24 to 0:31 (7 seconds)
Subject: aerial drone shot of empty Manhattan skyline at dawn
Action: camera slowly pushes forward, slight downward tilt
Framing: wide establishing shot
Lighting: golden hour, low sun from frame-right
Mood: melancholy, pre-storm
Transition out: slow cross-fade to next
Audio note: ambient wind, no music yet
```

### Deep (~45 minutes)
Medium + reference image generation per scene. Each shot gets a visual reference (Nano Banana keyframe) the user reviews before any video generation begins.

### Production (~2-4 hours)
Deep + full visual style locking + sample i2v render of one scene + user approval gate before mass production. This is the safety pattern Nick called out — never spend on full production without user approval of the look.

## 4. The sample-then-confirm pattern (load-bearing rule)

This is the most important pattern in this skill. The agent never proceeds from storyboard to mass image/video generation without locking style with the user.

### The 4 commit gates

**Gate 1 — Style lock (BEFORE storyboarding)**
The agent confirms or proposes the visual style profile before writing a single shot. Pulls from the Channel Profile (Skill 05) if reference exists, otherwise asks: *"Before I storyboard — what's the visual feel you want? I can suggest based on your niche, or you can give me a reference channel."*

**Gate 2 — Storyboard text approval (BEFORE keyframe generation)**
Once the storyboard text is written, the agent surfaces it to the user. *"Here are 18 shots planned. Read through, tell me anything that feels off. Once locked, I'll generate keyframes."* No keyframes generated until user approves.

**Gate 3 — Sample keyframe approval (BEFORE all keyframes)**
Even after storyboard approval, before generating ALL keyframes, the agent generates ONE sample keyframe (typically Shot 1 or the most visually-defining shot). *"Here's the look I'd produce. This is the visual style. Approve to generate the remaining 17, or tell me what to change."*

**Gate 4 — Sample i2v approval (BEFORE all i2v renders)**
Once keyframes are approved, before generating all video clips, the agent renders ONE 5-second i2v sample of the most motion-defining shot. *"Here's how the motion will feel. Approve to render the rest."* This is the most expensive gate to skip — i2v at $0.084-0.500/sec adds up fast.

If any gate produces a no, the agent regenerates and re-surfaces. The agent never proceeds without explicit approval at each gate. Cost protection + quality protection.

## 5. The Storyboard Profile artifact

The structured output of a storyboard task. Lives in the project workspace, gets consumed by image generation, i2v generation, editor.

```
Storyboard — [video title]
Generated: [timestamp]
Depth: [light / medium / deep / production]
Style locked: [yes / no — references the Channel Profile]
Total shots: [N]
Total duration: [target seconds]

—— SECTION 1: STYLE LOCK ——
Visual style profile pulled from Channel Profile or established for this video:
- Color grade: [warm sepia / cool cinematic / clinical / saturated]
- Lighting register: [soft / hard / cinematic / available]
- Composition rules: [rule of thirds / center / split / experimental]
- Aspect ratio: [16:9 / 9:16 / 1:1]
- Reference channel match: [if applicable]
- Reference style images: [URLs or generated examples]

—— SECTION 2: SHOT LIST ——
For each shot:
- Shot number
- Timestamp range (start to end)
- Duration (seconds)
- Subject (what's in frame)
- Action (what moves)
- Camera (framing + movement)
- Lighting note
- Mood note
- Color grade override (if different from style lock)
- Transition out
- Audio note (music sync, SFX, ambient)
- Source: keyframe reference image URL once generated

—— SECTION 3: BEAT-LOCK NOTES (music videos only) ——
- BPM
- Beat-aligned cut timestamps
- Hook return points
- Drop / transition moments

—— SECTION 4: B-ROLL LIST (if applicable) ——
Lighter version of shots — just visual concepts paired to script timestamps

—— SECTION 5: TRANSITIONS PLAN ——
Across all shots — what types of transitions, in what frequency. Cuts vs fades vs wipes vs match cuts.

—— SECTION 6: APPROVAL LOG ——
Gate 1 (Style lock): [user approved at timestamp]
Gate 2 (Storyboard text): [user approved at timestamp]
Gate 3 (Sample keyframe): [user approved at timestamp]
Gate 4 (Sample i2v): [pending / approved]
```

## 6. Niche-specific storyboard approaches

### Music videos / drill / propaganda (brick-narrative storytelling style)

- **Beat-locked timing.** Every shot aligned to BPM. For 136 BPM songs, beat lands every 441ms. Shots typically span 4-8 beats (1.7-3.5 seconds).
- **Hook return = visual return.** Every chorus/hook reuses or echoes the same visual treatment — that's how the track builds visual identity.
- **Verse 1 vs Verse 2 differentiation.** Verse 1 introduces visual world. Verse 2 escalates — same world, more action, faster cuts.
- **Bridge = visual reset.** A different look or location for the bridge breaks pattern, then returns to chorus visual.
- **Outro = single sustained image** or slow zoom out.
- **Total shot count** for a 3-minute drill song: typically 40-70 shots.

### What-if shorts / Roblox-style verticals

- **Aspect ratio 9:16** mandatory.
- **Cascading consequence visualization.** Each line of dialogue gets one visual decision. Roblox/game-style stylization expected.
- **Hook visual at 0:00-0:03** (within the first beat — must hold attention before scroll).
- **Total shot count** for 60-90 sec short: typically 8-15 shots.

### News-hijack documentary (investigative-journalism, geopolitics documentary, medical-authority)

- **B-roll heavy, not full storyboard.** The host narration carries the structure; B-roll punctuates.
- **Document overlays** where evidence is presented. The agent records WHERE in the script document/screenshot evidence appears.
- **Cinematic interludes** at major reveals — full storyboard for those moments only.

### History / explainer with visualization (long-form mystery-documentary, tech-industrial-history visualization sections)

- **Mid-tier shot count** — script has narration spine, but key historical moments get full visualization.
- **Map / chart sequences** are scripted shot-by-shot.
- **Photo restoration scenes** get keyframes.

### Ambient / sleep / focus loop

- **Single sustained scene.** No real storyboard. Style lock only.
- **The "shot" is a visual concept** — "rainy library at night, candles, slow-tilt camera over 2 hours."

## 7. Style locking — the prerequisite step

Before any storyboarding work, the agent locks visual style. Three paths:

### Path A — Channel Profile already exists
User has shipped 3+ videos. Channel Profile (Skill 05) has Visual Style DNA. Agent loads it. Done.

### Path B — Reference channel
User says "make it look like a long-form mystery-documentary channel." Agent runs Skill 05 ingestion (medium-deep), pulls Visual Style DNA, applies anchor differentiation. Surfaces the proposed style to user. Locks on approval.

### Path C — Niche-only inference
User has no Channel Profile yet, no reference. Agent infers from niche conventions (e.g., music video → cinematic moody, what-if short → Roblox-stylized, news-hijack → document-overlay heavy). Surfaces 2-3 style proposals to user with sample reference images. User picks.

The agent never storyboards from a vague style. *"Cinematic" is not a style. "Warm sepia, single key light, rule-of-thirds composition, slow cuts" is a style.*

## 8. Beat extraction — script to scene mapping

For scripts with continuous narration (vs music videos), the agent maps script beats to storyboard shots:

**Step 1 — Read the full script.**
**Step 2 — Identify natural beat boundaries:**
- Topic shifts
- Sentence-of-the-paragraph that introduces a new idea
- Rhetorical pauses
- "And then..." / "What happened next..." transitions
**Step 3 — Estimate timestamp for each beat** (using ~150 wpm narration speed).
**Step 4 — Allocate one shot per beat by default.** Exceptions:
- Long beats (>15 sec) get 2-3 shots
- Punchy beats (<3 sec) may share a shot with the surrounding beat
**Step 5 — Surface the beat-shot map to user before generating keyframes.**

For music video scripts (lyrics):
- Each bar = 4 beats
- Default 1 shot per 4-8 bars (4-second to 8-second shot length at 136 BPM)
- Hook lines get reusable shots
- Drop moments get distinct visuals

## 9. Shot type vocabulary

The agent uses a controlled vocabulary so downstream tools (image gen, i2v models) understand intent.

### Camera framing
- Extreme close-up (XCU) — eyes only, single object detail
- Close-up (CU) — face only, hand and small prop
- Medium close-up (MCU) — head and shoulders
- Medium shot (MS) — waist up
- Wide shot (WS) — full body, room
- Extreme wide shot (EWS) — landscape, scale
- Insert — object detail (document, prop)
- Aerial / drone — overhead
- POV — first person
- Over-the-shoulder (OTS) — character interaction

### Camera movement
- Static — no movement
- Pan — horizontal rotation
- Tilt — vertical rotation
- Push in / pull out — toward/away from subject
- Dolly — physical movement
- Tracking — following subject
- Crane — vertical
- Whip pan — fast pan, often as transition
- Arc — circular movement around subject

### Lighting registers
- High-key — bright, even, low contrast
- Low-key — dark, dramatic, high contrast
- Three-point — standard
- Available / natural — no rigging
- Practical — visible light sources in frame
- Silhouette — backlit subject
- Underlit — light from below (creepy register)
- Color-keyed — single dominant color (red room, blue night)

### Color grade descriptors
- Warm sepia / cool cinematic / clinical bright / saturated pop / muted documentary / desaturated grit / film noir / neon

### Transitions
- Hard cut — instant
- Match cut — visual continuity across cut
- Cross-fade — overlap
- Whip pan — fast pan blends two shots
- Wipe — directional reveal
- Smash cut — fast cut to dramatically different scene
- Dissolve — slow blend

The agent uses these terms when describing shots so the i2v model interprets correctly.

## 10. Duration math

For music videos:
- 4 beats = 1 bar
- 1 bar duration (sec) = 60 / BPM × 4
- At 136 BPM: 1 bar = 1.76 sec
- Standard shot length: 4-8 bars (7-14 sec) at 136 BPM
- Very fast cuts: 1-2 bars (1.7-3.5 sec)
- Sustained sections: 8-16 bars (14-28 sec)

For narration:
- Standard B-roll cut: 3-5 seconds (matches average sentence)
- Cinematic establishing shots: 7-10 seconds
- Fast B-roll punctuation: 1-2 seconds
- Avoid shots under 1 second (read as "fast cut" stylistically — only use deliberately)

For i2v constraints:
- Most i2v models cap at 5-10 seconds per generation
- Shots longer than 10 sec require either two consecutive i2v generations stitched, OR a sustained-camera-move single render, OR alternating to a different shot type at the 10-sec mark

The agent factors model constraints into duration decisions.

## 11. Anti-patterns

**A1 — Storyboarding talking-head content.** Wastes time. The "shot" is the host. Skip storyboard.

**A2 — Skipping style lock.** Generating keyframes before user approves the visual style. Result: user hates the look, agent burns budget regenerating.

**A3 — Generating all keyframes before sample approval.** Even with style locked, individual keyframe quality varies. Always sample first.

**A4 — Vague shot descriptions.** "Show a guy in a suit" is not a shot. The agent always specifies framing + lighting + mood + duration.

**A5 — Beat misalignment in music videos.** Shots that don't land on beats produce visual-audio dissonance. The agent always math-checks against BPM.

**A6 — Forgetting the hook return.** Music video chorus/hook should reuse or echo verse 1's visual register so brand identity reinforces. Don't generate fresh visuals every chorus.

**A7 — Over-cutting.** More than ~30 cuts/min in non-music content reads frenetic. Less than 6 cuts/min reads dull. The agent targets niche conventions.

**A8 — Style drift mid-storyboard.** Shot 1 is sepia; Shot 14 is neon-cyberpunk. Style lock applies to ALL shots unless a deliberate visual shift is part of the structure (bridge in music video).

**A9 — Ignoring i2v duration limits.** Storyboarding 20-second sustained shots when the model caps at 10 sec. Plan within constraints.

**A10 — Skipping the approval log.** If gates pass without explicit user approval, the agent has no record and can't roll back cleanly.

## 12. Worked examples

### Example 1 — Brick-narrative storytelling music video, "You're Not Jesus"

- **Style lock (Gate 1):** Reference channel = past brick-narrative storytelling episodes. Visual Style DNA: cinematic moody, saturated graded, brick-character world, mid-pace cuts. User approves.
- **BPM:** 136. Total track length 3:30 = 210 sec. Bar duration 1.76 sec. Total bars: 119.
- **Storyboard depth:** Production
- **Total shots:** 52 (avg shot length ~4 seconds, varies)
- **Beat structure:**
  - Hook (intro, 8 bars, 14 sec): 4 shots
  - Verse 1 (16 bars, 28 sec): 7 shots
  - Chorus (8 bars, 14 sec): 4 shots — REUSES hook visual register
  - Verse 2 (16 bars, 28 sec): 7 shots — escalates from V1
  - Chorus (8 bars, 14 sec): 4 shots — same hook register
  - Bridge (8 bars, 14 sec): 4 shots — visual RESET, distinct register
  - Chorus (8 bars, 14 sec): 4 shots — return to hook register
  - Outro (8 bars, 14 sec): 1 sustained zoom-out shot
- **Shot list snippet (Shot 1):**
  ```
  Shot 01 — 0:00 to 0:03.5 (3.5 sec, 2 bars)
  Subject: brick-toy crowd in town square, mid-density, neutral expressions
  Action: slow camera push-in toward central figure
  Framing: WS establishing
  Lighting: cinematic, golden hour key from frame-right
  Mood: ominous calm before storm
  Color grade: warm saturated cinematic
  Transition out: hard cut on downbeat
  Audio note: hook line drops on cut
  ```
- **Sample keyframe (Gate 3):** Generated for Shot 1 via Nano Banana. User approves the look.
- **Sample i2v (Gate 4):** Generated 5-sec sample of Shot 1 via LTX-2.3. User approves motion. Mass production proceeds.

### Example 2 — Roblox-scenario short, "What If A Teacher Owned Roblox?"

- **Style lock:** Reference = past Roblox-scenario shorts. Visual Style DNA: 9:16 vertical, Roblox-stylized, saturated, fast cuts, mid-pace.
- **Total duration:** 75 seconds
- **Storyboard depth:** Medium
- **Total shots:** 11
- **Shot list snippet:**
  ```
  Shot 01 — 0:00 to 0:05 (5 sec)
  Subject: stern adult teacher in Roblox-stylized classroom
  Action: zoom on teacher's face as scene transitions to Roblox HQ logo
  Framing: MCU
  Mood: deadpan-comedic
  Audio: "BRO! Imagine if a teacher OWNED Roblox..." narration begins
  ```
- **Gates 1-2:** User approves style + shot list.
- **Gate 3:** Sample keyframe Shot 1. User approves.
- **Gate 4:** Sample i2v 5-sec for Shot 1. User approves. Production proceeds.

### Example 3 — News-hijack documentary B-roll list (light depth)

- **Decision:** Light storyboard only — narration drives, B-roll punctuates.
- **No Gate 3 / Gate 4 sample required because keyframes are stock-footage-driven, not generative.**
- **B-roll list:**
  ```
  [00:30] B-roll — Chase Bank exterior, modern day, daylight
  [01:15] B-roll — generic phone showing incoming call screen
  [02:00] B-roll — close-up of bank document being filled out
  [03:45] B-roll — historical footage of 1970 bank security legislation signing
  [05:20] Document overlay — FinCEN Form 112 with key fields highlighted
  ```

## 13. Runtime checklist

- [ ] Decided whether storyboard is needed (decision flow §2)
- [ ] Style locked at Gate 1 with user approval
- [ ] Shot list written at chosen depth
- [ ] Beat math validated (music videos: BPM × bar length × shot count = total duration)
- [ ] Shot list approved at Gate 2 with user explicit OK
- [ ] Sample keyframe generated, approved at Gate 3
- [ ] Sample i2v generated, approved at Gate 4 (production depth only)
- [ ] All shots fit within i2v model duration limits
- [ ] Transitions plan locked
- [ ] Approval log timestamped at every gate

If any gate fails, regenerate. Never bulk-generate without sequential approval.

---

## Update log

This skill is current as of April 2026. Update when:
- New i2v models change duration limits or style capabilities
- Music video / propaganda niche conventions evolve
- New depth tier emerges (e.g., real-time AI live storyboarding)
