companions.body:
# Skill 02 Companion — Thumbnail Composition Bank

This is the runtime companion to Skill 02 (Thumbnail Design). Skill 02 names the 12 patterns and describes them in prose. This file gives the agent the **pixel-level composition spec** for each pattern — exact subject placement, face position, text placement, color anchors, contrast targets — plus a bank of worked image-gen prompts.

The agent loads this when generating thumbnail keyframes. Instead of inventing composition each time, it cites the pattern's locked spec and adapts the topic into it.

Coordinate convention used throughout: 1280×720 canvas (YouTube standard). Coordinates given as `(x_pct, y_pct)` from top-left, so `(33%, 33%)` is the upper-third intersection (top-left rule-of-thirds anchor).

---

## 1. Why pixel-level specs matter

Most thumbnail advice is verbal: "put the face on the left, add a number in the corner." That's not enough for an AI agent generating images at scale. Two thumbnails that follow the same verbal rule can look completely different — one wins, one fails — because the actual pixel placement, contrast ratio, or text size landed differently.

A locked composition spec collapses that variance. The agent generates within the spec, and the spec is calibrated to the patterns that actually win in production.

The four metrics every spec controls:
1. **Focal hierarchy** — what the eye lands on at 0ms, 100ms, 300ms
2. **Mobile legibility** — readable at 480×270 (small mobile feed thumbnail size)
3. **Contrast budget** — luminance separation between subject and background, target ≥ 4.5:1 for text, ≥ 3:1 for primary subject
4. **Color anchor** — the single saturated color that pulls the eye in feed

---

## 2. Pixel-level composition specs (P1-P12)

### P1 — Face + Arrow + Number

**Canvas zones:**
- **Face:** left third. Eyes positioned at `(28%, 38%)` — slightly above the rule-of-thirds top intersection. Head occupies ~45% of canvas height. Shoulders cut at bottom edge.
- **Arrow:** mid-frame, originating from face's gaze direction, terminating at `(67%, 50%)`. Arrow color = same as the bright accent (red or yellow).
- **Number:** upper-right corner. Anchored at `(85%, 22%)`. Font size = 22-28% of canvas height (180-200px on a 720 canvas). White or yellow with thick black stroke (8-12px).
- **Background:** dark, low-saturation. The bright accent (face skin tone, arrow, number) does the lifting.

**Color anchors:** primary red `#E63946` or yellow `#FFD60A` on a `#1A1A1A` to `#2D2D2D` dark background.
**Contrast target:** number text contrast ≥ 7:1 against background. Face-to-background luminance ratio ≥ 5:1.
**Mobile readability:** number must read at 240×135. Test by squinting at 25% zoom — number is the survivor.

**Worked image-gen prompt:**
> "Photoreal thumbnail composition. Left third of frame: middle-aged white male, age approximately 50, short professional grey hair, navy suit, expression of concerned authority looking slightly off-camera to the right. Eyes at upper-third position. Background: dark gradient navy to black. No text, no graphics — text and graphics will be added in code. Cinematic key light from camera-left. 1280x720. Subject head occupies left 40% of frame, right 60% intentionally empty negative space for graphics overlay."

The arrow and number are added in code (Remotion / Photoshop / SVG overlay), never in the image-gen prompt.

### P2 — Rage Stamp

**Canvas zones:**
- **Stamp text block:** centered or upper-center, anchored at `(50%, 35%)`. Tilted 8-12° counter-clockwise. Text size = 28-35% of canvas height. Three-word maximum (e.g., "MUCH WORSE", "CONFIRMED", "SHOCKING").
- **Background subject:** face-in-shock OR object-of-rage centered behind the stamp at lower opacity (60-70%). Subject occupies bottom 60% of canvas.
- **Stamp color:** saturated red `#D62828` or yellow `#FFB627` text, white inner stroke (4px), thick black outer stroke (10-14px).
- **Distress treatment:** texture overlay on stamp at 15-25% opacity. Edges roughed via clipping mask.

**Color anchors:** primary red `#D62828` on a desaturated background. Background subject treated cool (cyan-shifted) so red pops.
**Contrast target:** stamp text ≥ 9:1 against any underlying area.
**Mobile readability:** stamp must dominate at 240×135. Subject is supportive; stamp is the click.

**Worked image-gen prompt (background subject):**
> "Photoreal background image for thumbnail composition. Centered: middle-aged Caucasian woman, age 65, expression of shocked alarm, mouth slightly open, looking directly at camera with wide eyes. Hair grey, neutral blouse. Background: out-of-focus interior of a bank or government office, warm lighting from windows. Cinematic, slightly desaturated. 1280x720. Note: text and graphic stamp will be added in code, leave upper-third clear for overlay."

The stamp is added in code with the tilt, stroke, and distress treatment.

### P3 — Before/After Split

**Canvas zones:**
- **Vertical split:** divider at exactly `x = 50%`. Sometimes diagonal (8-12° tilt) for energy.
- **Before (left):** desaturated, slightly cool-shifted, often with red X overlay at `(25%, 25%)`. Subject framed centered in left half.
- **After (right):** vibrant, slightly warm-shifted, green check at `(75%, 25%)`. Subject framed centered in right half.
- **Optional center arrow:** anchor at `(50%, 50%)`, arrow body 12-15% of canvas width.

**Color anchors:** red `#D62828` and green `#06A77D` for the X and check. Subjects retain natural color but with saturation/temperature differential.
**Contrast target:** the after-side luminance ≥ 1.4× the before-side luminance. Eye reads the brighter side as "good."
**Mobile readability:** the split must be visible at 240×135. The X and check are the secondary read.

**Worked image-gen prompt (each side generated separately and composited):**
> "Photoreal thumbnail half-frame, vertical orientation 640x720. Subject: middle-aged man, age 45, slumped posture, defeated expression, dim grey lighting, slightly desaturated, cool color grade. Wearing wrinkled white shirt. Background: dim interior, single overhead bulb. Cinematic, intentionally muted."

> "Photoreal thumbnail half-frame, vertical orientation 640x720. Subject: same middle-aged man, age 45, confident upright posture, faint smile, golden-hour warm lighting, vibrant saturation. Wearing crisp white shirt. Background: bright clean office, large windows, golden light. Cinematic, intentionally vibrant."

The two halves are composited in code with the X, check, and arrow overlays.

### P4 — Mystery Object

**Canvas zones:**
- **Object:** centered, anchored at `(50%, 55%)` — slightly below mathematical center. Object occupies 35-50% of canvas height.
- **Background:** dark, atmospheric, with deliberate negative space at top 30% and bottom 15%.
- **Lighting:** single key light from camera-left or above. Rim light optional. The object is the only well-lit thing in frame.
- **Text:** typically NONE on the thumbnail itself. Title carries the mystery.
- **Optional:** small specific anchor (a date, a location text element) bottom-right at `(85%, 88%)`, ~6% of canvas height.

**Color anchors:** monochrome or near-monochrome. Single accent color from the object itself (lit warm against cool dark, or lit cool against warm dark).
**Contrast target:** object-to-background luminance ratio ≥ 6:1. Background should be near-black except for the object's spill.
**Mobile readability:** the object's silhouette must be recognizable at 240×135. Test by converting to silhouette — does it still read?

**Worked image-gen prompt:**
> "Cinematic thumbnail. Single subject centered slightly below midline: an antique brass key, oxidized, lying on weathered wooden surface. Single warm key light from upper-left, deep shadow filling rest of frame. Dark moody atmosphere, charcoal-to-black background gradient. Shallow depth of field, sharp focus on key. No text, no graphics. 1280x720. Style of long-form mystery-documentary thumbnail. Photoreal, slightly cinematic film grain."

### P5 — Reaction Face

**Canvas zones:**
- **Face:** centered at `(50%, 45%)` — slightly above mathematical center. Face occupies 60-75% of canvas height. Eyes at `(50%, 30-35%)` for direct eye contact lock.
- **Optional single word:** lower third, anchored at `(50%, 80%)`. Word size ~18-22% of canvas height. Examples: "WHAT?!", "NO WAY", "$1M".
- **Background:** vibrant solid color OR slight gradient. Often complementary to skin tone (yellow background for reddish skin, blue for warmer skin).

**Color anchors:** vibrant background color (yellow `#FFD60A`, magenta `#E63987`, cyan `#3DA5D9`) — the saturation IS the click trigger.
**Contrast target:** background-to-face contrast ≥ 4:1. Face well-lit from front.
**Mobile readability:** the expression must read at 240×135. Closed-mouth shock reads better than open-mouth at small sizes.

**Worked image-gen prompt:**
> "Bright vibrant thumbnail. Centered subject: young woman, age 25, expression of stunned disbelief — closed mouth, raised eyebrows, eyes wide. Front-lit with even soft light. Looking directly at camera. Background: solid saturated yellow #FFD60A. Subject occupies upper 70% of frame. Lower 25% intentionally empty for text overlay. 1280x720. Photoreal, top viral-challenge thumbnail style."

### P6 — Authority Portrait

**Canvas zones:**
- **Subject:** centered or rule-of-thirds left. Eyes at `(33%, 38%)` if left-anchored, `(50%, 35%)` if centered. Head occupies 40-55% of canvas height. Three-quarter view often, sometimes direct.
- **Background:** office, library, studio. Out-of-focus. Single key light, soft. Often warm-grade.
- **Text:** if any, lower-third small caps title in clean sans-serif. Anchored at `(50%, 88%)`, max 6% of canvas height.
- **Color treatment:** muted, professional, often slightly cool-graded with warm skin tones for separation.

**Color anchors:** restrained — navy `#1A2A4F`, charcoal `#2D2D2D`, cream `#F5F0E1`. The lack of saturation IS the brand signal.
**Contrast target:** subject-to-background contrast ≥ 3:1. Underplays loud thumbnails on purpose.
**Mobile readability:** the face's authority register must be readable. Eye contact + steady expression is the click.

**Worked image-gen prompt:**
> "Editorial portrait thumbnail. Subject: middle-aged Asian man, age 55, distinguished, three-quarter view facing camera, calm authoritative expression, neutral closed mouth, salt-and-pepper hair, navy suit, no tie. Background: out-of-focus library or office interior, warm muted lighting. Single soft key light from camera-left. Photoreal, slightly cinematic. 1280x720. Style of science-explainer or long-form interview thumbnail. No text."

### P7 — Stacked Number Pile

**Canvas zones:**
- **Stack:** dominant lower 65% of canvas. Anchored at `(50%, 70%)`. Stack height = 50-60% of canvas height. Stack should breathe — visible perspective and dimensionality, not flat.
- **Optional host:** rule-of-thirds left, pointing at the stack. If present, host occupies 30-35% of left side.
- **Number callout:** upper-right at `(80%, 22%)`, large. Text size = 25-30% of canvas height.
- **Background:** clean, slightly desaturated, often with a single bright color anchor on the stack itself.

**Color anchors:** stack color is the protagonist. If stack is money/cash → green `#06A77D`. Stack is products → vibrant single product color.
**Contrast target:** stack-to-background contrast ≥ 4:1. Number callout ≥ 7:1.
**Mobile readability:** the stack must read as "lots of [things]" at 240×135. Quantity-shorthand is the read.

**Worked image-gen prompt:**
> "Photoreal thumbnail. Bottom 60% of frame filled with a chaotic but organized pile of one-hundred dollar bills, three-dimensional perspective, slight overhead angle. Stack overflowing forward toward viewer. Bright even lighting. Background: clean white-to-light-grey gradient. Upper 35% of frame intentionally empty for number overlay. 1280x720. Photoreal, top viral-challenge or host-led real-estate thumbnail style."

### P8 — Negative-Space Word

**Canvas zones:**
- **Word:** dominant, filling 55-65% of canvas. Anchored at `(50%, 50%)`. Single word — never two. Examples: "REVEALED", "BANNED", "$0", "DEAD".
- **Background:** solid color or simple gradient. NO subject, NO objects.
- **Optional micro-element:** small icon or tiny secondary detail at `(50%, 80%)` or `(85%, 15%)`. Adds depth without breaking the negative-space rule.

**Color anchors:** two-color maximum. Often white-on-black, black-on-yellow, or red-on-white.
**Contrast target:** word ≥ 12:1 against background. The pattern lives or dies on contrast.
**Mobile readability:** word readable at 120×68 (extreme mobile feed thumbnail size).

**Image-gen prompt:** typically NOT generated by AI — assembled in vector code (SVG / Remotion / Figma export). The font choice, kerning, and sub-pixel rendering matter too much for image generation.

**Spec instead:**
> Background: solid `#FFD60A` yellow. Text: "BANNED" in Bebas Neue Bold or similar industrial display, kerning -2%, vertically and horizontally centered. Color `#1A1A1A`. Optional thin black stroke 2px. 1280x720.

### P9 — Split Frame

**Canvas zones:**
- **Vertical split:** at `x = 50%`. Often a thin border (4-8px) between halves, often white or accent color.
- **Left subject:** anchored at `(25%, 50%)`.
- **Right subject:** anchored at `(75%, 50%)`.
- **Optional vs/and label:** centered at `(50%, 88%)` or floating between subjects.
- **Color treatment:** halves often opposite-graded (left warm + right cool, or left bright + right muted).

**Color anchors:** complementary colors. Background of left and right halves intentionally different.
**Contrast target:** each half ≥ 4:1 internal contrast. Inter-half differential ≥ 1.5× luminance.
**Mobile readability:** the comparison-fact must read at 240×135. Each subject identifiable at small size.

**Worked image-gen prompt (compose two halves separately):**
> Left: "Photoreal thumbnail half-frame 640x720. Apple iPhone Pro on white background, top-down product shot, vibrant saturation, warm lighting."
> Right: "Photoreal thumbnail half-frame 640x720. Samsung Galaxy on dark background, top-down product shot, cool blue lighting."

Composite in code with thin white divider and "VS" label.

### P10 — Color-Pop on Mono Background

**Canvas zones:**
- **Color element:** rule-of-thirds anchored at `(33%, 50%)` or `(67%, 50%)`. Element occupies 25-40% of canvas.
- **Background:** desaturated entirely (≤ 8% saturation). Color element is the only saturated thing.
- **Optional small text:** upper-right or lower-left, sub-anchor, ~8% of canvas height.

**Color anchors:** ONE saturated color, period. Often red `#D62828` or yellow `#FFD60A` on a sepia/grey/charcoal mono background.
**Contrast target:** color element saturation ≥ 80% vs background ≤ 8%. Massive saturation differential.
**Mobile readability:** the colored element must dominate at 240×135 even when desaturated background is muddy.

**Worked image-gen prompt:**
> "Photoreal thumbnail. A single red apple in sharp focus, anchored on left third at `(33%, 50%)`, vibrant saturation. Surrounding scene: photoreal kitchen counter, but rendered entirely in desaturated grey-sepia, near-monochrome. Apple is the only colored object. Cinematic, slightly graded. 1280x720. Documentary thumbnail style. No text."

### P11 — Photoreal Composite

**Canvas zones:**
- **Subject:** rule-of-thirds anchored, often with multiple composited elements.
- **Background:** dramatic environment, often impossible (interior cathedral with explosion, courtroom with stack of money, etc.).
- **Lighting:** cinematic, often three-point (key + fill + rim), graded for emotional register.
- **Text:** if any, integrated into the scene (sign, paper, etc.) rather than overlaid.

**Color anchors:** cinematic color grade. Cool blue `#1B3B6F` for somber, orange `#E76F51` for action, green `#06A77D` for money/legal.
**Contrast target:** ≥ 5:1 between subject and background. Lighting contrast ≥ 3:1 between key and shadow.
**Mobile readability:** the dramatic scene must communicate the topic at 240×135. Test by viewing at 25%.

**Worked image-gen prompt:**
> "Cinematic photoreal composite thumbnail. Foreground left: middle-aged Caucasian woman, age 60, expression of resigned worry, holding a folded letter. Background: dimly lit American kitchen, mail scattered on counter, single overhead bulb. Through window, distant view of a federal building (US Treasury or Capitol). Color grade: cool blue-gray with warm interior accent. Cinematic depth of field. 1280x720. No text. Style of HBO documentary thumbnail."

### P12 — AI-Generated Surreal

**Canvas zones:**
- **Subject:** often rule-of-thirds, sometimes deliberately off-center for dreamlike feel.
- **Background:** impossible perspective, dreamlike rendering, dramatic light angles.
- **Text:** typically NONE — surreal aesthetic is the click. If text, integrated into the surreal scene.

**Color anchors:** highly saturated, often neon or cinematic graded. Specific to the channel's locked aesthetic.
**Contrast target:** ≥ 5:1 between focal subject and background environment.
**Mobile readability:** the surreal vibe must read at 240×135 — abstract enough to look distinctive, concrete enough to be recognizable.

**Caution:** post-Jan 2026 YouTube enforcement — surreal AI thumbnails on authority/finance/health channels trigger inauthentic-content concerns. Use only on channels where surreal IS the genre (music videos, art channels, AI-creative).

**Worked image-gen prompt:**
> "Surreal cinematic thumbnail. Centered: a giant rotary telephone, photoreal but impossibly large, sitting in the middle of an empty desert at sunset. Sky: dramatic orange-to-purple gradient. Long shadow extending toward camera. Slight tilt-shift effect. Hyperreal saturation, slight film grain. 1280x720. Style of brick-narrative storytelling or surreal music video thumbnail. No text."

---

## 3. Cross-pattern composition rules

These apply regardless of which pattern the agent picks.

### The 3-zone hierarchy

Every thumbnail has three readable elements at maximum:
- **Primary:** the eye lands here at 0-100ms. The face, the stamp, the object, the word.
- **Secondary:** the eye lands here at 100-300ms. Number, arrow, supporting subject.
- **Tertiary:** the eye lands here at 300ms+ if curiosity is engaged. Channel branding, small text, micro-detail.

If a thumbnail has a fourth readable element competing for attention, drop it. The primary loses to noise.

### The mobile-first crop test

Every thumbnail must work at:
- **480×270** (mobile feed standard)
- **240×135** (mobile suggested truncation)
- **120×68** (desktop sidebar suggested)

The agent renders the thumbnail and tests readability at each size. If primary readability fails at 240×135, the thumbnail is rejected.

### The face hierarchy rule

When using face-based patterns (P1, P5, P6):
- **Closed-mouth shock outperforms open-mouth shock** at small sizes by ~12% CTR (vidIQ 2024). Open-mouth reads as "yelling" at 240×135 and turns viewers off.
- **Direct eye contact outperforms gaze-off** by ~8% CTR for authority content; **gaze-off outperforms direct** by ~6% for mystery/forensic content.
- **Face-cropped-tight outperforms face-with-shoulders** by ~10% on mobile feed.

### The text-in-code rule (mandatory)

NEVER ask the image-gen model to render text. AI models render text inconsistently — kerning, font, stroke all degrade. Text is added in code (Remotion / SVG / Photoshop) on top of the generated image.

This is the same rule as Skill 09 §2. It's mandatory for all thumbnail generation.

### The "saturated thumb test"

Place the candidate thumbnail next to 11 random YouTube thumbnails (from the actual feed of the target audience). Does the candidate stand out at the macro scale, not just the micro scale? If the candidate blends into the field, the color anchor or composition is wrong.

### The contrast budget

Every thumbnail has a contrast budget. Spend it on the primary read. Spending it on three competing elements means none win.

- **High-contrast accents:** ≤ 1 per thumbnail (the bright stamp, the number, the colored object).
- **Mid-contrast support:** 2-3 elements.
- **Low-contrast atmosphere:** the background.

If the agent finds itself making four high-contrast elements, the composition is failing. Pick ONE primary anchor.

---

## 4. Anti-pattern bank

Six thumbnails that look correct at first glance but fail in production. Diagnoses attached.

### Anti-pattern A — *The Six-Element Cluttered Frame*

Face + arrow + number + stamp + secondary subject + small caption text. Everything competing.
**Why it fails:** No clear primary read. Mobile eye bounces between elements at 240×135 and registers nothing.
**Fix:** Strip to 3 elements. Pick primary (face), secondary (number), tertiary (channel logo). Drop everything else.

### Anti-pattern B — *Open-Mouth Yelling Face Against Loud Background*

Subject with mouth wide open, screaming, against a saturated yellow + red striped background.
**Why it fails:** Reads as 2018 BuzzFeed clickbait; the retain-cohort skips reflexively. Mouth shape pixelates at 240×135 into a black hole.
**Fix:** Closed-mouth shock with slightly raised eyebrows. Calm the background to one anchor color.

### Anti-pattern C — *AI-Generated Text on the Image*

The image-gen model rendered the title onto a sign, a banner, or a chalkboard within the scene. Text shows visible AI artifacts (warped letters, inconsistent kerning).
**Why it fails:** Triggers post-July-2025 inauthentic content signals; viewers reject AI-rendered text on sight.
**Fix:** Generate the image with NO text. Add text in code. Mandatory.

### Anti-pattern D — *Cinematic Mystery Object on a Vibrant Yellow Background*

Pattern-mismatched composition. The mystery object pattern (P4) calls for moody dark backgrounds; pasting a moody object on a saturated yellow is pattern-confused.
**Why it fails:** The viewer sees "loud thumbnail = entertainment register" and clicks for entertainment, then the video is somber documentary. Click-cohort mismatch destroys retention.
**Fix:** Match composition register to content register. Documentary = dark moody. Entertainment = bright vibrant. Don't cross-pollinate.

### Anti-pattern E — *Five Faces in a Row*

Reaction-face panel with 5 different reactions stacked horizontally. Looks like a meme template.
**Why it fails:** Mobile feed renders this as a noisy strip with no readable face. None of the 5 faces is large enough at 240×135.
**Fix:** One face. Make it big. The pattern is P5 Reaction Face, not P5 Reaction-Faces-Plural.

### Anti-pattern F — *Tiny Text on a Busy Photoreal Background*

12-word title rendered in 4% canvas-height text on top of a complex photoreal scene.
**Why it fails:** Text fails the mobile readability test at 240×135. Primary read is unclear because no element dominates.
**Fix:** Either drop the text entirely (let title carry it) or make it dominant (P8 Negative-Space Word) on a clean background.

---

## 5. Per-niche composition recommendations

The patterns work in any niche, but the **dominant pattern** and the **color anchor** vary. Quick reference:

| Niche | Dominant patterns | Color anchor | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| Senior finance / IRS | P2, P11, P1 | Red `#D62828` or yellow `#FFD60A` | Rage register — closed-mouth concern, never smiling. |
| Senior health | P11, P6, P2 | Warm `#E76F51` or muted teal | Closed-mouth concern, doctor-credentialed look. |
| Tech / AI | P6, P10, P8 | Charcoal `#2D2D2D` + single accent | Calm authority. NO loud colors, NO ALL CAPS in text. |
| History | P4, P11, P10 | Cinematic warm-cool gradient | Dark moody. Object-focus. Long-form mystery-documentary aesthetic. |
| News-hijack docs | P11, P2, P5 | Cool blue `#1B3B6F` + red accent | Cinematic forensic. Investigative-journalism style. |
| Vertical shorts | P5, P1, P8 | Vibrant background | Big face, big single word. Native Shorts aesthetic. |
| Music video / propaganda | P12, P11 | Saturated cinematic grade | AI-surreal acceptable here; locked channel aesthetic. |
| True crime | P4, P11, P10 | Cool desaturated | Restrained, weighted. Never sensational. |
| Cooking | P3, P5, P11 | Warm food tones | Bright food shots. Closed-mouth host satisfaction. |
| Real estate | P3, P11, P1 | Warm interior + green money | Before/after dominant. House thumbnail = aspirational. |
| Faith | P6, P10, P4 | Cream / muted gold | Reverent. NO ALL CAPS. NO bright stamps. |
| Doc long-form | P10, P6, P4 | Restrained mono + accent | Tech-industrial-history, logistics-explainer style. |

---

## 6. The composition spec at runtime

When the agent generates a thumbnail:

1. **Identify pattern** from Skill 02 §3 + niche match (this companion §5).
2. **Load composition spec** from this file's §2 for that pattern.
3. **Generate image-gen prompt** following the worked example, with explicit "no text, no graphics" instruction.
4. **Render image** at 1280×720.
5. **Add text and graphics in code** using the spec's coordinates and color anchors.
6. **Run the saturated thumb test** — render against 11 niche-typical thumbnails and check standout.
7. **Run the mobile crop test** — verify primary read at 480×270, 240×135, 120×68.
8. **Run the contrast budget audit** — ensure ≤ 1 high-contrast accent.
9. **Run the anti-pattern check** — verify the thumbnail does not match patterns A-F in §4.
10. **Surface to user with composition citation** — show which pattern was used and which spec was applied.

If any check fails, regenerate the failing element. Never surface a thumbnail that fails the contrast or mobile-crop test.

---

## 7. When to consult this file vs Skill 02

**Load Skill 02 when:** picking the pattern, understanding the niche playbook at the strategy level, learning the color theory rules, learning the face-and-emotion theory.

**Load this companion when:** generating the image-gen prompt, calculating where to place text/graphics in code, auditing a candidate thumbnail against composition specs, debugging a thumbnail that "looks fine" but feels wrong.

The two files are complementary: Skill 02 = strategy + theory; this file = pixel-level execution.

data.body:
# Skill 01 — Title Creation

This is the operational knowledge an AI YouTube agent needs to produce the perfect title for any video in any niche. Every paragraph is a concrete rule the agent can cite and apply.

---

## 1. The job of a title

A title is a contract. The viewer reads it, predicts what they'll get, and clicks if the predicted payoff exceeds their alternatives in that 30-second feed-scrolling moment. Every title makes a promise. Every video has to pay that promise off within the first 30 seconds or watch-time collapses and the algorithm punishes the next upload.

The agent's job is to produce a title that:
- **Wins the click** against ~12 competing thumbnails on a mobile screen
- **Previews the satisfaction** the video delivers (a clickbait-only title hurts the channel within 24 hours)
- **Signals to the algorithm** what topic and audience this video is for, so it gets surfaced to the right cohort

The agent never optimizes for click-through rate alone. The 2025-2026 algorithm judges every video on **CTR × AVD × Satisfaction**. A 20% CTR with 30% retention loses to a 7% CTR with 65% retention.

Quote from YouTube's Senior Director of Growth & Discovery, Todd Beaupre: *"If we showed everyone the most clickable thumbnail and got 20% CTR but the video only delivered for 5% of viewers, we'd be optimizing for the wrong thing."* This is the single most important sentence in title strategy as of 2025.

## 2. The optimization target

The agent optimizes titles against **predicted watch-time-per-impression**, not raw CTR. This is the metric YouTube uses internally and the metric YouTube's native Test & Compare feature uses to pick the winner of an A/B test.

Predicted watch-time-per-impression for a candidate title is a function of:
- **CTR potential** — does the title win the click against the niche median?
- **Hook alignment** — does the title set up a payoff the script's first 30 seconds can deliver?
- **Audience fit** — does the title attract the cohort that retains, not the cohort that bounces?
- **Niche pattern fit** — does the title match what works in this specific niche?

A title that nails all four metrics is "watch-time positive." A title that nails only CTR is "click-trap" and burns the channel.

The agent's mental model: "Will this title generate 8 minutes of watched content per 100 impressions?" Not "will this title generate 12 clicks per 100 impressions?"

## 3. The 13 canonical title formulas

Every winning title in 2025-2026 fits one of these 13 formulas, or combines two of them. The agent generates 12 variants per video using a spread across formulas, then ranks by predicted watch-time-per-impression.

### F1 — Em-Dash Mystery Gap

**Structure:** `[Specific concrete claim] — [Mystery payoff at 75-85% position]`

**Examples:**
- *Why Banks Fear Customers Who Keep $20,000 in Cash — The Account Clause Nobody Reads*
- *$160,000 Gone In One Phone Call — Why Chase Won't Give It Back*
- *He Built A $40M Business — Then Lost It In 90 Days*

**When to use:** Any niche with a story arc or a hidden mechanism. Strongest for finance, true crime, history, science.

**When NOT to use:** Pure how-to / educational tutorials where the payoff has to be in the title for SEO.

**Why it works:** The em-dash creates a curiosity gap. The first half makes a concrete promise. The second half teases a hidden answer. Mobile feed truncation tests show the em-dash often falls at the visibility cutoff, which forces the user to click to see the resolution.

**Expected lift:** Em-dash titles outperform colon titles by approximately 10-15% CTR in the same A/B condition (Spotter Studio data, 2024).

### F2 — Specific Dollar Number

**Structure:** `[$X amount] [verb] [outcome] — [optional mystery]`

**Examples:**
- *$246,000 Gone By Filing Social Security At 70 (Most Retirees Don't Know This)*
- *I Spent $1M On A Single Trade — Here's What Happened*
- *$32,820 Seized. Zero Charges Filed.*

**When to use:** Finance, business, real estate, retirement, lifestyle income claims. Works in any niche where a dollar figure conveys stakes.

**When NOT to use:** Niches where money discussion feels off-brand (faith, parenting, comedy).

**Why it works:** Specific dollar numbers are processed differently by the brain than vague qualifiers. "$32,820" is more click-worthy than "thousands of dollars" because the specificity signals authority and concreteness. Spotter Studio data: numbered titles outperform unnumbered titles by 36% on average.

**Critical rule:** Use odd, specific, "discovered" numbers (7, 13, 23, 47) over round, "manufactured" numbers (10, 20, 50). Odd numbers feel real. Round numbers feel marketed.

### F3 — Counter-Narrative

**Structure:** `[Conventional wisdom statement] — [Why it's wrong] / [Numbered reasons]`

**Examples:**
- *These 7 REASONS Will Make You File Social Security at Age 62 (NOT 70)*
- *Stop Investing In Index Funds — Do This Instead*
- *Why "Drink 8 Glasses of Water" Is Wrong*

**When to use:** Any niche where there's a dominant "everyone says X" assumption you can credibly subvert. Especially powerful when you have credentials.

**When NOT to use:** When you can't actually subvert the wisdom credibly. The video has to deliver. A counter-narrative that doesn't pay off creates immediate dislikes.

**Why it works:** The brain is wired to attend to information that contradicts existing beliefs (negativity bias + curiosity gap). Counter-narrative titles also attract a higher-intent audience that engages more.

### F4 — Numbered List

**Structure:** `[N] [things] [verb] [outcome]`

**Examples:**
- *5 Banking Rules That Just Got MUCH WORSE*
- *7 Things Every Retiree Must Do Before May 1*
- *13 Foods That Reverse Type 2 Diabetes (Per a specialist doctor)*

**When to use:** Almost any niche. The numbered list is the most reliable formula in YouTube history.

**When NOT to use:** Story-led documentaries where a list undermines the narrative.

**Why it works:** Numbered titles signal video structure. The viewer knows there will be N discrete chapters. Retention improves because the viewer commits to watching all N. Spotter Studio: numbered titles see 36% higher CTR and 22% higher AVD vs comparable unnumbered titles.

**Number selection rules:**
- 3-7: highest CTR (small enough to feel digestible)
- 9-13: high authority (feels comprehensive)
- 17, 23, 47: unusual numbers spike CTR via novelty
- 10, 20, 50: avoid — too manufactured-feeling

### F5 — Named Villain

**Structure:** `[Brand/person] [is doing X to Y] — [stakes]`

**Examples:**
- *Why Chase Won't Give Your Money Back After A Wire Transfer Scam*
- *Coinbase Is Quietly Locking Customer Accounts — Here's Why*
- *The IRS Just Changed Three Rules That Will Cost Retirees Thousands*

**When to use:** Finance, scam-exposure, news-hijack, true crime. Any time you have a credible institutional villain.

**When NOT to use:** When the villain framing is exaggerated. If the institution is more nuanced than "evil," the video feels like clickbait when it gets there.

**Why it works:** A named entity creates an immediate audience identification ("I bank with Chase, I need to know") and a clear emotional register (rage). Named villain titles consistently outperform abstract titles in finance and scam-exposure niches.

### F6 — Threat Alert

**Structure:** `[CONFIRMED / URGENT / WARNING]: [specific threat] [time anchor]`

**Examples:**
- *CONFIRMED: Social Security Shake-Up Hits May 1*
- *WARNING: New IRS Rule Takes Effect In 30 Days*
- *URGENT: Three Bank Closures Coming Before Year-End*

**When to use:** News-hijack, time-sensitive content, regulatory changes, deadline-driven episodes.

**When NOT to use:** Evergreen content. The threat-alert format burns out fast — use sparingly so the audience doesn't tune out the urgency signal.

**Why it works:** Combines deadline framing + authority framing + curiosity gap. The audience reads "CONFIRMED" as "the news is real" and "shake-up" as "I need to know what." A reference episode in this niche used this format and pulled significant outlier numbers.

### F7 — Forensic / Story-Led

**Structure:** `[Specific person] [verb past tense] [shocking outcome] — [hint at how]`

**Examples:**
- *He Lost $160,000 In One Phone Call — Then Chase Refused To Refund Him*
- *She Filed Social Security At 62 And Saved $246,000 — Here's How*
- *They Lost Their Restaurant After A Bank Filed One Form*

**When to use:** Single-victim narrative episodes. Strongest in finance, true crime, business, scam-exposure.

**When NOT to use:** Educational tutorials.

**Why it works:** The brain attends to specific human stories more than abstractions. A specific named or pronoun-led subject ("She," "He," "They") creates instant character investment.

### F8 — Question + Implied Answer

**Structure:** `Why does [counter-intuitive thing happen]? / What happens when [scenario]?`

**Examples:**
- *Why Do The Wealthy Never Pay Estate Tax?*
- *What Happens If You Withdraw $10,001 From Your Bank?*
- *Why Are Boomers Selling Their Homes In 2026?*

**When to use:** Educational, science, history, finance. Especially the science-explainer style of educational content.

**When NOT to use:** When you can't actually answer the question definitively. A question title that ends with "...it's complicated" kills future channel trust.

**Why it works:** Open-ended questions activate cognitive curiosity. But: question titles only outperform declaratives when the question is genuinely puzzling. Generic questions ("Why is X important?") underperform.

### F9 — Quote Attribution

**Structure:** `[Authority figure name]: "[Provocative claim]"`

**Examples:**
- *John Bogle: Why Banks Fear Customers Who Keep $20,000 In Cash*
- *Warren Buffett: The Investment Mistake That Cost Me $200 Billion*
- *Top Creator: How I Lost $30M In 2024*

**When to use:** When you have a real or credibly-paraphrased quote from an authority figure. Common in faceless / AI-narration channels.

**When NOT to use:** When the quote is fabricated. Audiences are increasingly sensitive to fabricated authority quotes; YouTube's July 2025 inauthentic content policy specifically targets fake attribution.

**Why it works:** Borrowed authority. The clicker assumes the figure said something true and important. Strong CTR mechanism but high satisfaction risk.

### F10 — Wound-First

**Structure:** `[Painful stakes statement to viewer] — [How to fix]`

**Examples:**
- *Your Retirement Will Run Out By Age 78 If You Do This*
- *You're Losing $4,000 A Year On This One IRS Mistake*
- *Your Doctor Won't Tell You About This Test*

**When to use:** Health, finance, retirement, parenting. Any niche where the audience has a specific worry the title names.

**When NOT to use:** Lifestyle, comedy, vlog. The wound-first frame doesn't fit aspirational content.

**Why it works:** Names the viewer's specific anxiety. Direct second-person ("You") outperforms third-person in CTR by approximately 10-12% (Backlinko 2024 study).

### F11 — Bracketed / Parenthetical Tag

**Structure:** `[Main title] [(Specific Modifier)]` or `[Main title] [BRACKETED LABEL]`

**Examples:**
- *5 Investing Mistakes That Cost Me $1M (Genius Strategy)*
- *I Tried Apple's New AI [HONEST REVIEW]*
- *The 2026 Social Security Schedule [UPDATED]*

**When to use:** Tech reviews, finance content, listicles. Bracketed tags signal video format and add a second curiosity gap.

**When NOT to use:** Faith, comedy, ambient. The bracketed format reads marketed.

**Why it works:** Brackets and parens consistently lift CTR by 15-38% vs identical unbracketed versions (vidIQ 2024 data). The bracket creates a second visual hook the eye lands on.

### F12 — ALL CAPS Authority

**Structure:** `[1-3 ALL CAPS WORDS] [rest of title in normal case]`

**Examples:**
- *CONFIRMED: Social Security Shake-Up Hits May 1*
- *The 10,000 Dollar Bank Rule Just Got MUCH WORSE*
- *URGENT: Three Banks To Avoid In 2026*

**When to use:** Senior finance, scam-exposure, news-hijack, threat-alert. Any niche where rage or urgency is the dominant emotional register.

**When NOT to use:** Tech, science, history, education, faith, comedy. ALL CAPS in these niches reads spammy and CTR craters.

**Why it works:** ALL CAPS signals urgency and authority simultaneously. The eye lands on caps first; if the rest of the title pays off, the click follows.

**Strict cap on ALL CAPS usage:** No more than 30% of the total title characters should be in caps. More than that triggers the spam-pattern recognition both in viewers and in YouTube's own ranking signals.

### F13 — How-To / Tutorial Direct

**Structure:** `How To [outcome] In [time/effort frame]`

**Examples:**
- *How To Read Your Social Security Statement In 5 Minutes*
- *How To Set Up A Trust In One Afternoon*
- *How To Spot An IRS Phishing Email*

**When to use:** Educational, tutorial, software, productivity, any niche where SEO match is critical.

**When NOT to use:** Story-led, narrative, opinion. How-to is the lowest CTR formula on average but the highest SEO-discoverability formula.

**Why it works:** Direct match to user search query. How-to titles win Search and Suggested traffic but underperform on Browse (the main feed).

## 4. Character count discipline

The agent sizes titles for the surface they'll appear on. There are five surfaces with different truncation cutoffs:

| Surface | Truncation cutoff | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Mobile feed (browse) | 50-60 chars | The first scroll. Most CTR happens here. |
| Mobile suggested (after-watch sidebar) | 35-45 chars | Brutal truncation. The first 5 words must carry the click. |
| Mobile search results | 50-60 chars | Same as mobile feed. |
| Desktop feed | 60-70 chars | More forgiving but desktop is <30% of total views in 2026. |
| TV / connected TV | 70+ chars (entire title shown) | Growing surface, especially for senior demos. |

**The "first 5 words" rule:** Whatever curiosity gap, dollar number, or named villain drives the click MUST be in the first 5 words. If it falls after position 5, mobile users never see it.

**Bad:** *Here's How A Couple In Iowa Lost $32,820 To The IRS — The Forfeiture Loophole*
**Good:** *$32,820 Seized — How An Iowa Grandmother Lost Her Restaurant To The IRS*

The dollar number anchors at position 1 in the second version. Truncation safe.

**Em-dash placement rule:** When using F1 (Em-Dash Mystery Gap), the dash should fall at 75-85% of total title length. Too early and the mystery payoff feels rushed. Too late and the dash gets truncated on mobile.

**Total length sweet spot:** 55-65 characters. Long enough for keywords. Short enough for mobile suggested truncation. Most outlier titles in 2025-2026 fall in this range.

## 5. ALL CAPS, em-dash, and emoji rules

### ALL CAPS

| Niche | ALL CAPS use | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Senior finance / IRS | Heavy | Rage frame is the dominant emotional register. CONFIRMED, MUCH WORSE, NOW work. |
| News-hijack docs | Heavy | URGENT, BREAKING, CONFIRMED |
| Scam exposure / fraud | Heavy | EXPOSED, REVEALED, BANNED |
| True crime | Moderate | Single-word emphasis only (KILLED, FOUND) |
| Tech / AI | None | Reads spammy. Tech audience punishes with low CTR. |
| Science / science-explainer | None | Authority is gentle, not loud. |
| History | None | The long-form mystery-documentary / deadpan-history styles are calm and mysterious. |
| Health / medical | Light | DOCTOR REVEALS works. Excessive caps feel pseudoscience. |
| Real estate | Light | Specific words like SOLD, BANNED ok. |
| Beauty / fashion | None | Reads aggressive. |
| Cooking | None | Warm tone. |
| Vlog / lifestyle | None | Personal, not screaming. |
| Crypto | Heavy | Speculation niche. CONFIRMED, BREAKING, BANNED. |
| How-to / education | None | SEO-optimized titles read calmer. |
| Fitness / bodybuilding | Moderate | SHREDDED, RIPPED, MAX work. |
| Faith / Christian | None | Tone is reverent. |
| Politics | Heavy | Rage frame. SHOCKING, EXPOSED, BANNED. |
| Travel | None | Aspirational tone. |
| Comedy / shorts | Light | Single-word emphasis only. |
| Reaction | Moderate | INSANE, UNREAL work. |
| Documentary long-form | None | Tech-industrial-history, logistics-explainer, and engineering-explainer channels — all calm titling. |
| Music video | Light | Track names sometimes get caps. |
| Ambient / sleep | None | Calm aesthetic. |

### Em-dash

The em-dash (—) is the highest-CTR punctuation in YouTube titles in 2025-2026. It outperforms the colon by approximately 10-15% in matched A/B tests.

Use rules:
- **Position at 75-85% of title length.** Forces mystery payoff.
- **Use a true em-dash (—), not a hyphen (-) or two hyphens (--).** Mobile rendering matters.
- **One em-dash per title.** Two reads choppy.
- **Don't pair with a colon.** Pick one.

When NOT to use em-dash: pure tutorial / how-to titles, where the title needs to read as a search query.

### Emoji

**Default: never.** Emojis in YouTube titles in 2026 read spammy and trigger pattern recognition both in viewers and in moderate algorithm signals.

Narrow exceptions:
- 🔥 in fitness / hype gym content (single emoji, end of title only)
- 💰 in some finance hype channels (but our brand is authority, so no)
- 🚨 in extreme news-hijack (use only when CONFIRMED format isn't fitting)
- ⚠️ in compliance / legal warning content

The agent's default behavior is to never include emoji. Add only on explicit user request, and only one emoji per title.

## 6. Niche-specific playbooks

The agent loads the relevant playbook based on the channel's declared niche. Every playbook includes: top 3 winning formulas, character count target, ALL CAPS posture, em-dash usage, real example titles.

### Senior finance / IRS / retirement (personal-finance authority channel brand)
- **Top formulas:** F12 ALL CAPS Authority, F2 Specific Dollar Number, F4 Numbered List, F1 Em-Dash Mystery
- **Char count:** 55-70
- **ALL CAPS:** Heavy (CONFIRMED, MUCH WORSE, NOW)
- **Em-dash:** Yes, at ~75% position
- **Examples:**
  - *The 10,000 Dollar Bank Rule Just Got MUCH WORSE*
  - *CONFIRMED: Social Security Shake-Up Hits May 1*
  - *Why Banks Fear Customers Who Keep $20,000 In Cash — The Account Clause Nobody Reads*

### Tech / AI / dev tools (style of major tech-review and dev-tool channels)
- **Top formulas:** F8 Question, F11 Bracketed Tag, F13 How-To
- **Char count:** 45-65
- **ALL CAPS:** None — punishes CTR
- **Em-dash:** Light (single em-dash for review-style titles)
- **Examples:**
  - *Apple's M5 Pro Reviewed — Honestly*
  - *Why Claude Code Beats Cursor (For Now)*
  - *Building An MCP Server In 10 Minutes*

### Gaming / Roblox / Minecraft / Fortnite
- **Top formulas:** F4 Numbered List, F8 Question, F1 Em-Dash Mystery
- **Char count:** 40-55 (mobile-heavy audience, brutal truncation)
- **ALL CAPS:** Light (single-word emphasis only)
- **Em-dash:** Yes
- **Examples:**
  - *I Built The Largest Minecraft Castle Ever*
  - *What If A Teacher OWNED Roblox?*
  - *5 Roblox Games Banned In 2026 — Why?*

### Music videos / propaganda / drill (brick-narrative storytelling style)
- **Top formulas:** Track-name title primarily, F9 Quote Attribution secondarily
- **Char count:** 25-50
- **ALL CAPS:** Light (track names sometimes ALL CAPS)
- **Em-dash:** Rare
- **Examples:**
  - *"You're Not Jesus!" Iran Drops Another Brick Music Video*
  - *Antichrist - Iran Music Video (Official Music Video)*

### News-hijack documentary (investigative-journalism / geopolitics documentary style)
- **Top formulas:** F6 Threat Alert, F5 Named Villain, F1 Em-Dash Mystery
- **Char count:** 55-70
- **ALL CAPS:** Moderate (BREAKING, EXPOSED, CONFIRMED)
- **Em-dash:** Yes
- **Examples:**
  - *He Stole $40 Million From Crypto Investors — Now He's Free*
  - *EXPOSED: How OpenAI Lobbies Against Open Source*

### True crime
- **Top formulas:** F7 Forensic Story-Led, F1 Em-Dash Mystery, F8 Question
- **Char count:** 50-65
- **ALL CAPS:** Light (single emphasized words)
- **Em-dash:** Yes
- **Examples:**
  - *She Vanished On Her Honeymoon — Then The Husband Confessed*
  - *The Detective Who Solved 47 Cold Cases In 6 Months*

### Health / medical / supplements (doctor-personality / medical-authority style)
- **Top formulas:** F10 Wound-First, F4 Numbered List, F8 Question
- **Char count:** 50-65
- **ALL CAPS:** Light (DOCTOR REVEALS works as single phrase)
- **Em-dash:** Light
- **Examples:**
  - *7 Foods That Reverse Type 2 Diabetes (Per a specialist doctor)*
  - *Why Your Doctor Won't Tell You About This $4 Test*
  - *Your Joints Hurt Because Of This One Supplement Mistake*

### Real estate / home (host-led real-estate creator style)
- **Top formulas:** F2 Specific Dollar Number, F4 Numbered List, F11 Bracketed Tag
- **Char count:** 50-65
- **ALL CAPS:** Light
- **Em-dash:** Light
- **Examples:**
  - *I Bought A House For $1 (Honest Review)*
  - *5 Cities Where Home Prices Will CRASH In 2026*

### Beauty / fashion / makeup
- **Top formulas:** F4 Numbered List, F11 Bracketed Tag, F8 Question
- **Char count:** 40-55
- **ALL CAPS:** None
- **Em-dash:** Light
- **Examples:**
  - *5 Makeup Trends That Aged Me 10 Years*
  - *Honest Review: The $400 Cream Everyone's Buying*

### Cooking / food (technique-led cooking channels)
- **Top formulas:** F13 How-To, F8 Question, F11 Bracketed Tag

- **ALL CAPS:** None
- **Em-dash:** Light
- **Examples:**
  - *I Tried The $200 Steakhouse Method At Home*
  - *Perfect Carbonara In 8 Minutes (Italian Approved)*

### History / explainer (long-form mystery-documentary / deadpan-history / side-project history channels)
- **Top formulas:** F1 Em-Dash Mystery, F7 Forensic, F8 Question
- **Char count:** 50-65
- **ALL CAPS:** None — calm authority is the brand
- **Em-dash:** Yes
- **Examples:**
  - *The Map Of Europe In 1346 — And Why It Looked Like This*
  - *Why Roman Concrete Still Works (And Modern Doesn't)*

### Science (science-explainer / science-animation channels)
- **Top formulas:** F8 Question, F1 Em-Dash Mystery, F13 How-To
- **Char count:** 45-60
- **ALL CAPS:** None
- **Em-dash:** Yes
- **Examples:**
  - *Why Quantum Computers Don't Work The Way You Think*
  - *The Math Problem That Broke A 200-Year Streak*

### Vlog / lifestyle
- **Top formulas:** F7 Forensic, F8 Question
- **Char count:** 40-60
- **ALL CAPS:** None
- **Em-dash:** Light
- **Examples:**
  - *I Lived In A Tesla For 30 Days*
  - *The Day I Quit My $200K Job*

### Crypto / finance trading
- **Top formulas:** F6 Threat Alert, F2 Specific Dollar Number, F5 Named Villain
- **Char count:** 50-65
- **ALL CAPS:** Heavy (BREAKING, BANNED, EXPOSED)
- **Em-dash:** Yes
- **Examples:**
  - *BREAKING: Coinbase Just Locked $400M In Customer Funds*

### How-to / education
- **Top formulas:** F13 How-To, F4 Numbered List
- **Char count:** 50-65

### Fitness / bodybuilding
- **Top formulas:** F4 Numbered List, F2 Specific Number, F10 Wound-First
- **Char count:** 45-60
- **ALL CAPS:** Moderate (SHREDDED, RIPPED, MAX)
- **Em-dash:** Light
- **Examples:**
  - *I Lost 30 Pounds In 90 Days — Here's My Exact Diet*
  - *5 Exercises That Build SHREDDED Abs In 4 Weeks*

### Faith / Christian / religion
- **Top formulas:** F8 Question, F7 Forensic Story
- **Char count:** 50-65
- **ALL CAPS:** None — reverent tone
- **Em-dash:** Light
- **Examples:**
  - *Why The Early Church Met On Sundays (Not Saturdays)*
  - *The Verse That Changed Everything For Me*

### Politics / commentary
- **Top formulas:** F12 ALL CAPS Authority, F5 Named Villain, F6 Threat Alert
- **Char count:** 55-70
- **ALL CAPS:** Heavy (SHOCKING, BANNED, EXPOSED)
- **Em-dash:** Yes
- **Examples:**
  - *EXPOSED: What Congress Just Hid In The 2026 Budget*

### Travel
- **Top formulas:** F2 Specific Number, F10 Wound-First (mild), F8 Question
- **Char count:** 40-60

  - *I Spent $50 In Tokyo For A Week*
  - *Why Bali Isn't Worth It Anymore*

### Comedy / shorts (Roblox-scenario style)
- **Top formulas:** F8 Question (especially "What if..."), F4 Numbered List
- **Char count:** 30-50 (vertical feed, brutal truncation)
- **ALL CAPS:** Light
- **Em-dash:** Rare
- **Examples:**
  - *What If A Teacher OWNED Roblox?*
  - *I Tried Every Mountain Dew Flavor*

### Reaction
- **Top formulas:** F7 Forensic, F8 Question
- **Char count:** 35-55
- **ALL CAPS:** Moderate (INSANE, CRAZY, UNREAL)
- **Em-dash:** Light

  - *INSANE Reaction To A Top Creator's $1M Stunt*
  - *I Watched The Top Podcast's New Episode — Here's My Take*

### Documentary long-form (tech-industrial-history / logistics-explainer / engineering-explainer channels)
- **Top formulas:** F1 Em-Dash Mystery, F8 Question, F7 Forensic
- **Char count:** 50-70
- **ALL CAPS:** None
- **Em-dash:** Yes
- **Examples:**
  - *How Taiwan Builds Half The World's Chips — The TSMC Story*
  - *The Industry That Disappeared In 6 Years*

### Ambient / sleep / focus loop
- **Top formulas:** Descriptive title only (no formulas)
- **Char count:** 40-65
- **ALL CAPS:** None
- **Em-dash:** Light
- **Examples:**
  - *Cozy Library Rain Sounds for Deep Sleep — 8 Hours*
  - *Lofi Hip Hop Mix to Study to (No Ads)*

## 7. The competitor mining protocol

Before generating a title for any video, the agent must study the niche. This is a 7-step protocol the agent runs in approximately 30 seconds:

**Step 1 — Pull top 20 outlier titles** in the same niche from the last 90 days. Define outlier as views > 3× channel median.

**Step 2 — Tag each title with formula(s) used.** Each title may use 1-2 of the 13 canonical formulas. Tag accordingly.

**Step 3 — Frequency analysis.** Which formulas appear in more than 30% of outliers? That's the dominant niche pattern. Generate primarily from that pattern.

**Step 4 — Character count cluster.** What's the median title length among outliers? The agent's generated titles should fall within ±5 characters of this median.

**Step 5 — ALL CAPS frequency.** What percentage of outlier titles use ALL CAPS? Match the distribution.

**Step 6 — Em-dash frequency.** Same analysis. Don't introduce em-dashes if outliers don't use them.

**Step 7 — Build the niche "title DNA" template.** A structured record:
```
Niche: [name]
Median character count: [X]
Top 3 formulas: [F1, F4, F12]
ALL CAPS frequency: [X%]
Em-dash frequency: [X%]
Common phrases / power words: [list]
Common villains: [list]
```

This DNA template is then loaded as system-prompt context for the title generation step.

## 8. The generation workflow

The agent generates titles using a YouTube growth strategist's discipline: **always produce 12 candidates, never fewer.** This is the working number top growth strategists use for top creators.

**Step 1 — Read the script + niche DNA.** Identify the hook architecture, the core promise, the satisfaction payoff, the specific numbers in the video.

**Step 2 — Generate 12 candidates** with deliberate spread across formulas:
- 3 from the niche's top formula
- 3 from the niche's secondary formula
- 2 from the niche's tertiary formula
- 2 wildcards (formulas not commonly used in the niche — sometimes the wildcard wins)
- 2 ALL-CAPS-and-em-dash maximalist versions

**Step 3 — Score each candidate.** Run the scoring rubric:
- Specific number present? +2
- Em-dash at 75-85% position? +2
- First 5 words carry the click? +3
- Character count 50-70? +2
- Niche formula match? +2
- ALL CAPS within 30% rule? +1
- Personal pronoun (I/you)? +1
- Anti-pattern penalties: -3 for each generic opener, click-trap, or cliché

**Step 4 — Surface top 3 + the wildcard.** Show the user the top 3 by score plus the wildcard. Always include the wildcard so the user has a non-obvious option.

**Step 5 — User picks or modifies.** User selects, edits, or asks for variation.

**Step 6 — Save the chosen title to channel memory.** The pattern that won this video becomes a higher-weighted candidate for the next video.

## 9. A/B testing discipline

YouTube's native Test & Compare runs for 4-14 days and judges variants on **watch-time-per-impression**, not raw CTR. The agent should default to setting up an A/B for every uploaded video.

**Test setup rules:**
- Use 2 variants by default. 3 if the script supports it.
- Variants should test different CTR mechanisms (e.g., one specific number, one mystery gap), not different word choices.
- Same thumbnail across variants. Title is the only variable.
- Same description, tags, scheduling, end screen.
- Don't touch for at least 7 days. Manual override only if CTR delta > 30% after 5 days.

**Watch-time-per-impression as the metric:** A title that pulls 18% CTR but loses on retention always loses to a title that pulls 11% CTR with strong retention. The agent should optimize for the latter.

## 10. Anti-patterns

Titles that fail across the board. The agent never generates these.

**A1 — Generic openers.** "How to be more productive," "5 tips for better health," "The truth about money." Vague + non-specific = ignored.

**A2 — Click-trap that doesn't pay off.** "$1 Billion Dollar Secret REVEALED" when the video shows a $5,000 lesson. Audience punishes within 30 seconds.

**A3 — Over-promising.** "This Will CHANGE YOUR LIFE." Promise too big, payoff impossible.

**A4 — Vague mystery.** "You won't believe what happened next." Curiosity gap with no specific anchor.

**A5 — Excessive ALL CAPS.** More than 30% of title characters in caps. Spam-pattern recognition.

**A6 — Emoji clutter.** "🚨 BREAKING 🔥 The IRS just BANNED 💰..." Reads as spam.

**A7 — Question-with-no-answer.** "Why is the economy collapsing? It's complicated." Dead-end.

**A8 — Year-stamping in evergreen titles.** "How to invest in 2024" dies on January 1, 2025. Use year only for genuinely time-locked content.

**A9 — Title-thumbnail mismatch.** Title says "5 reasons" and thumbnail shows a single face with no reference to 5. The pair has to be coherent.

**A10 — Channel name in title.** "[Channel Name] Reviews The 2026 Tax Code." Wastes characters; channel name is shown separately.

**A11 — Generic listicles with round numbers.** "10 best [thing]." Round numbers feel marketed.

**A12 — Subjunctive titles.** "What I Would Do If I Started Over." Subjunctive feels theoretical and underperforms.

**A13 — Self-referential titles.** "My biggest realization in 2026 was..." Audience doesn't care yet.

**A14 — Pure SEO titles.** "Best Investment Advisors For Retirees Near Me 2026" — reads robotic and underperforms on Browse, where most CTR happens.

## 11. The expert quote bank

Authority quotes the agent can cite when explaining its title decisions:

**Todd Beaupre, YouTube Senior Director Growth & Discovery:** "If we showed everyone the most clickable thumbnail and got 20% CTR but the video only delivered for 5% of viewers, we'd be optimizing for the wrong thing."

**A top viral-challenge creator:** "Title and thumbnail are 80% of the video's success. I spend more time on those two things than on the entire script."

**A YouTube growth strategist:** "Write 12 hooks. Always 12. The 13th is never the winner. It's almost always one of the first 5."

**A science-explainer channel host:** "There's a difference between legitbait — a title that promises something real and delivers — and clicktrap, which promises something real and doesn't. The algorithm in 2025 punishes clicktrap within 24 hours."

**A leading tech reviewer:** "In tech, you can't ALL CAPS your way to clicks. The audience reads it as inauthenticity. Calm titles with one specific claim consistently outperform."

**Sean Cannell (Think Media):** "The best titles answer a question the viewer didn't realize they had. The worst titles answer a question they're not asking."

**Hank Green:** "YouTube has always been about over-delivery. The title sets the expectation. The video has to crush it."

## 12. Worked examples

The agent applies the full skill in real time. Three examples of the skill in action:

**Example 1 — IRS Senior Finance, an example episode ($10K bank rule)**
- Niche: senior finance / IRS / retirement
- Hook architecture: Threat Alert + Counter-Narrative
- Niche DNA: F12 ALL CAPS Authority + F2 Specific Dollar Number heavy
- Generated candidates (the strategist's 12):
  1. *The 10,000 Dollar Bank Rule Just Got MUCH WORSE* ← winner
  2. 5 Banking Rules That Just Got MUCH WORSE — Every Retiree Must Know
  3. CONFIRMED: 5 Bank Rule Changes Take Effect This Week
  4. The 10K Bank Rule Has 5 New Updates — Here's What's Different
  5. ...
- Winner reasoning: F12 ALL CAPS + F2 Specific Number + character count 49 + first 5 words carry the click
- Outcome: This title pulled the highest single-day views in the channel's history

**Example 2 — Roblox-scenario Shorts**
- Niche: gaming / Roblox shorts
- Hook architecture: F8 Question
- Niche DNA: F8 Question dominant, mobile truncation brutal
- Generated:
  1. *What If A Teacher OWNED Roblox?* ← winner
  2. The Teacher Who Bought Roblox For $1
  3. Why Teachers Will Soon Own Roblox
- Winner reasoning: F8 Question + character count 32 + first 5 words carry the click + ALL CAPS on single word for emphasis (OWNED) without exceeding 30% rule

**Example 3 — Doctor Senior Health (medical-authority style)**
- Niche: health / medical / supplements
- Hook architecture: Wound-First + Counter-Narrative
- Niche DNA: F10 Wound-First + F4 Numbered List + light em-dash
- Generated candidates:
  1. *Your Joints Hurt Because Of This One Supplement Mistake* ← winner
  2. 5 Supplements That Make Joint Pain Worse (Per Dr. Williams)
  3. Why Glucosamine Doesn't Work — And What Does
- Winner reasoning: F10 Wound-First + direct second-person "Your" + character count 56 + specific anchor ("This One Supplement")

## 13. The agent's runtime checklist

Before surfacing any title to the user, the agent runs:

- [ ] Niche DNA loaded for this channel
- [ ] 12 candidates generated with formula spread
- [ ] Each candidate scored against the rubric
- [ ] Top 3 + wildcard selected
- [ ] Each surfaced title passes character count rule
- [ ] First 5 words carry the click
- [ ] ALL CAPS within 30% rule
- [ ] Em-dash positioned at 75-85% if used
- [ ] No anti-patterns present
- [ ] Title-thumbnail pair will be coherent
- [ ] A/B test plan ready (variants, duration, metric)

If any check fails, regenerate. Never surface a failing title.

---

## Update log

This skill is current as of April 2026. Update when:
- YouTube ships a new title-related feature (multi-language testing, dynamic titles, etc.)
- Algorithm changes shift CTR×AVD weighting
- A new niche emerges (e.g., AI-generated content has its own playbook now and should be added)
- New expert insights from top creators, growth strategists, or YouTube leadership become public

The raw research file at `projects/rookcast/knowledge/research/title-research-raw.md` is the source — quote it for primary sources when explaining decisions to the user.

companions.body:
# Skill 01 Companion — Title Bank, Outlier Autopsies & Anti-Patterns

This is the runtime companion to Skill 01 (Title Creation). Skill 01 documents the 13 formulas. This file gives the agent a deep, cite-able reservoir of:

1. **Per-niche title banks** — 8 worked titles per niche, annotated by formula and lift driver, for the 12 highest-priority niches
2. **Outlier title autopsies** — 8 real or composite titles dissected end-to-end, showing exactly why each one beat the niche median
3. **Anti-pattern bank** — 8 titles that look correct but fail, with the specific diagnosis

The agent loads this when generating title variants. Instead of inventing from formula in isolation, it pulls 3-5 closest-fit examples from the bank, then varies them through the topic. This is faster, higher quality, and produces less generic output.

Every annotated title is in the form:
> *Title text*
> Formula: F[N]. Lift driver: [the specific mechanism]. Watch-time positive because: [why the title attracts the retain-cohort, not the bounce-cohort].

---

## 1. Senior finance / IRS / retirement (a personal-finance authority channel)

The dominant niche for our system. Voice register is V2 Federal Credentialed Expert. Titles lean rage + threat + dollar specificity. Formulas F2, F5, F6, F10, F12 dominate.

**Bank:**

> *$246,000 Gone By Filing Social Security At 70 (Most Retirees Don't Know This)*
> Formula: F2 + F11 (parenthetical tag). Lift driver: specific dollar + counter-narrative tease. Watch-time positive because: the dollar figure is large enough to feel meaningful but specific enough to feel real, and the parenthetical promises the gap that retains.

> *CONFIRMED: Social Security Shake-Up Hits May 1*
> Formula: F6 + F12. Lift driver: ALL CAPS authority + named time anchor. Watch-time positive because: time anchor self-selects the audience that has Social Security and knows May 1 matters.

> *Why Banks Fear Customers Who Keep $20,000 In Cash — The Account Clause Nobody Reads*
> Formula: F1 + F5. Lift driver: em-dash mystery + named villain (banks). Watch-time positive because: the em-dash payoff (an actual clause) is deliverable, and the audience that clicks already keeps cash, which is the exact retain-cohort.

> *The IRS Just Changed Three Rules That Will Cost Retirees Thousands*
> Formula: F4 + F5. Lift driver: named villain + numbered list. Watch-time positive because: "three rules" sets a structural expectation; the audience commits to all three, lifting AVD.

> *He Lost $160,000 In One Phone Call — Then Chase Refused To Refund Him*
> Formula: F7 + F1. Lift driver: forensic story-led + em-dash. Watch-time positive because: single-victim narrative pulls the empathy click, not the rage click — empathy clickers retain longer.

> *Your Retirement Will Run Out By Age 78 If You Do This*
> Formula: F10. Lift driver: wound-first second-person. Watch-time positive because: "Age 78" is specific enough to make older viewers calculate against their own age, which is the exact internal commitment that sustains attention.

> *7 Things Every Retiree Must Do Before May 1*
> Formula: F4 + F6 (mild threat anchor). Lift driver: numbered list + deadline. Watch-time positive because: numbered titles average 22% higher AVD; the "before May 1" anchor self-selects time-sensitive viewers.

> *I'm A Federal Tax Accountant — Here's The Form That Stops Bank Levies*
> Formula: F1 + credentialed framing. Lift driver: credential + em-dash + specific solution. Watch-time positive because: the audience that clicks expects expert-grade specifics; matches the V2 Federal Credentialed Expert script voice.

---

## 2. Senior health / medical / supplements (medical-authority / doctor-personality health style)

Voice register is V2 medical variant or V8 Erudite Professor. Titles lean wound-first + counter-narrative. Formulas F3, F8, F10 dominate. ALL CAPS used sparingly.

**Bank:**

> *13 Foods That Reverse Type 2 Diabetes (Per a specialist doctor)*
> Formula: F4 + F9. Lift driver: numbered list + cited authority. Watch-time positive because: cited expert lifts trust; "reverse" is the click trigger; the article-style framing matches the audience's reading habit.

> *Why "Drink 8 Glasses Of Water" Is Wrong*

## Outlier title autopsies

Eight titles that beat their niche median by a measurable margin, dissected for the lift drivers.

### Autopsy 1 — *$246,000 Gone By Filing Social Security At 70 (Most Retirees Don't Know This)*

**Beat the niche median by:** ~3.2× CTR, ~1.8× AVD.
**Why it won:** Three click drivers stack — specific dollar ($246,000 not $250,000), counter-narrative (filing at 70 is conventional advice, the title says it's wrong), parenthetical inclusion claim ("most retirees" lets the viewer self-include). Each driver is independently strong; together they create CTR + audience-fit alignment.
**What to copy:** The triple-stack — specific number + counter-narrative + parenthetical inclusion.

### Autopsy 2 — *In 1518, 400 People Started Dancing And Couldn't Stop*

**Beat the niche median by:** ~4.5× CTR.
**Why it won:** Pure curiosity gap with mandatory click. Specific date + specific count + impossible-sounding event + cliff resolution. The brain cannot move past it without resolving. Title is 11 words but every word is doing work.
**What to copy:** Specific-date + specific-count + impossible-event combination for any history hook.

### Autopsy 3 — *He Lost $160,000 In One Phone Call — Then Chase Refused To Refund Him*

**Beat the niche median by:** ~2.8× CTR, ~2.1× AVD.
**Why it won:** The structure is forensic story-led + named institutional villain + em-dash mystery + audience-defining event (phone scam). Pronoun "He" pulls empathy click; "$160,000" anchors stakes; "Chase" names villain; em-dash structures the betrayal reveal.
**What to copy:** Pronoun-victim + dollar + named institution + em-dash structure for any single-victim finance episode.

### Autopsy 4 — *The Map That Shouldn't Exist*

**Beat the niche median by:** ~5× CTR (long-form mystery-documentary channels).
**Why it won:** Five-word title. Pure paradox premise. Mobile-feed truncation impossible to escape. Brain immediately asks "why shouldn't it exist?" and the only answer is to click. Best-in-class compression.
**What to copy:** When you have a single-paradox premise, compress to 5-7 words. Don't pad.

### Autopsy 5 — *I Spent $1M On A Single Trade — Here's What Happened*

**Beat the niche median by:** ~3× CTR (finance hype/skeptic crossover).
**Why it won:** First-person high-stakes claim + em-dash + open-ended outcome. The viewer doesn't know if it's a win or a loss, which is the key. If the title revealed the outcome, the click drops 40%.
**What to copy:** When the outcome is the click, never reveal it in the title. Stop at the action; let the open loop carry the click.

### Autopsy 6 — *13 Foods That Reverse Type 2 Diabetes (Per a specialist doctor)*

**Beat the niche median by:** ~2.5× CTR, ~2× AVD (health niche).
**Why it won:** Numbered list + medical claim + cited authority. Each component pulls a different click cohort: number-clickers (commit to all 13), reverse-claim-clickers (counter-narrative seekers), authority-clickers (research-trusters). The combined population is the largest health-niche click cohort possible.
**What to copy:** Numbered + medical-action-verb + cited-authority is the durable health title formula.

### Autopsy 7 — *Iran's TikTok Strategy Is A Brick Drill Music Video Factory*

**Beat the niche median by:** ~6× CTR (news-hijack baseline).
**Why it won:** Density. State actor + platform + medium + format compressed into 11 words. Every reader has to pause to decode the title, which is itself the click trigger. Density-titles work when each term is concrete; this title has zero abstraction.
**What to copy:** When titling a news-hijack with multiple unusual entities, do NOT smooth them into prose. Stack them. Let the density carry the click.

### Autopsy 8 — *The 1928 Cookbook That Predicted Modern Sourdough*

**Beat the niche median by:** ~2.3× CTR (cooking history crossover).
**Why it won:** Specific year + ordinary object (cookbook) + counterintuitive prediction. The combination of "1928" and "predicted" creates the curiosity gap; "modern sourdough" anchors current relevance.
**What to copy:** For any retrospective-history title, anchor with a specific year + ordinary object + counterintuitive future-pointing verb.

### Autopsy 9 — *Why The FDA Just Banned This $9 Supplement (Most Pharmacies Still Sell It)*

**Beat the niche median by:** ~3.6× CTR (senior health niche).
**Why it won:** Triple-stack: institutional villain (FDA banned) + dollar specificity ($9 — surprisingly small) + parenthetical contradiction ("most pharmacies still sell it" creates active dissonance). The contradiction is the curiosity engine — if the FDA banned it, why is it still on the shelf? Click-mandatory.
**What to copy:** Pair an institutional action (banned/ruled/changed) with a specific contradiction in the parenthetical. The contradiction is the click; the institution is the credibility.

### Autopsy 10 — *The Engineer Who Designed The 737 MAX Tried To Quit 11 Months Before The Crashes*

**Beat the niche median by:** ~5.2× CTR (news-hijack documentary).
**Why it won:** Forensic story-led + specific time anchor (11 months) + retrospective inevitability. The reader feels the "if only" energy before clicking; the specific 11-month figure signals investigative depth. Single-victim narrative with institutional scale stakes.
**What to copy:** When the retrospective-prophet figure is real and the documentation is on file, frame as "[role] tried to [warning verb] [specific time] before [disaster]." The specific duration is non-negotiable — vague "months" loses to specific "11 months."

### Autopsy 11 — *I Watched Every Episode Of [Show] And Counted How Many Times The Lawyer Lied*

**Beat the niche median by:** ~4.1× CTR (analysis / explainer crossover).
**Why it won:** Exhaustive-test framing ("every episode") + counter-narrative against the show's premise (lawyer is hero) + specific countable methodology ("counted how many times"). Promises forensic rigor on a beloved cultural object.
**What to copy:** Exhaustive-test format works when the dataset is bounded (every episode of a show, every claim in a campaign, every supplement in a class) AND the methodology is countable. Vague exhaustive-tests ("I tried lots of") fail; specific exhaustive-tests ("I tested all 47") win.

### Autopsy 12 — *My 84-Year-Old Mom Has Been Saving Bread Bag Tags For 60 Years. Here's Why She's Right.*

**Beat the niche median by:** ~3.8× CTR (lifestyle / personal-finance crossover).
**Why it won:** Personal narrative + age specificity (84) + duration (60 years) + counterintuitive defense ("here's why she's right" — preempting the reader's "that's hoarding" judgment). The defense-frame inverts what could be a cringe topic into vindication. Empathy click + curiosity click.
**What to copy:** When the surface-read of a title is "this seems weird/cringe/wrong," explicitly preempt with a defense framing. Don't ask "is X weird?" — declare "X is right" and earn it inside.

### Autopsy 13 — *Tesla's New Update Reset Every Battery I've Tested. Here's The Reading.*

**Beat the niche median by:** ~3× CTR (tech / dev tools-adjacent).
**Why it won:** Named villain (Tesla) + specific scope ("every battery I've tested" — implies many) + evidence promise ("here's the reading"). The reader expects data, not opinion. First-person investigation framing with branded specificity.
**What to copy:** For tech-criticism content, lead with the brand (not "this car company"), follow with personal-investigation scope, end with evidence-promise. Three-part structure that out-performs generic tech outrage.

---

## Anti-pattern bank

Eight titles that look correct, follow a formula, and still fail. Diagnosis attached.

### Anti-pattern 1 — *5 Tips To Improve Your Retirement*

**Formula on paper:** F4 (numbered).
**Why it fails:** Every word is generic. "Tips," "improve," "retirement" are all level-zero abstractions. No specific anchor, no dollar figure, no counter-narrative. The title says "I am a generic listicle." CTR craters.
**Fix:** Replace every abstract noun with a specific. *5 Things To Do Before May 1 If You're 62 Or Older* hits.

### Anti-pattern 2 — *EVERYTHING You NEED To KNOW About Social Security in 2026!!!*

**Formula on paper:** F12 (ALL CAPS).
**Why it fails:** ALL CAPS is overused; exclamation points compound the spam-pattern signal. Triggers viewer skip and algorithmic dampening simultaneously. "Everything you need to know" is the most generic possible promise.
**Fix:** Cap at one ALL CAPS word. Replace generic promise with specific. *CONFIRMED: 3 Social Security Changes Hit May 1* hits.

### Anti-pattern 3 — *Why I Stopped Drinking Coffee*

**Formula on paper:** F1-F8 ambiguous (sounds like a story).
**Why it fails:** The reason for the click is also the resolution. Once read, no curiosity remains. No specificity, no stakes, no counter-narrative. First-person without specific anchor.
**Fix:** Add a stake or a specific consequence. *Why I Stopped Drinking Coffee — And Lost 18 Pounds* hits.

### Anti-pattern 4 — *5 Things You Won't Believe About Banking*

**Formula on paper:** F4 (numbered).
**Why it fails:** "You won't believe" is a banned BuzzFeed-era phrase. Audiences read it as guaranteed clickbait. CTR among the retain-cohort drops sharply because the retain-cohort is the cohort most allergic to "you won't believe."
**Fix:** Replace with a specific. *5 Banking Rules That Just Got MUCH WORSE* hits.

### Anti-pattern 5 — *The Truth About AI Wrappers*

**Formula on paper:** F1 (em-dash variant) without the em-dash.
**Why it fails:** "The truth about" is the laziest possible promise. Sets up no specific question. The dev audience that would click an AI-wrapper take wants a specific thesis, not a generic reveal.
**Fix:** Replace with a specific thesis. *Why Most AI Wrappers Will Be Worth Zero In 18 Months* hits.

### Anti-pattern 6 — *URGENT WARNING — DO NOT IGNORE THIS RETIREMENT MISTAKE BREAKING NEWS!!!*

**Formula on paper:** F6 + F12 stacked.
**Why it fails:** Multiple urgency markers stacked (URGENT + WARNING + DO NOT + BREAKING) read as escalating spam. Formula stacking is a real failure mode — one urgency marker is the limit. Three is the spam pattern.
**Fix:** One urgency marker, max. *URGENT: New Retirement Rule Hits Before May 1* hits.

### Anti-pattern 7 — *Have You Ever Wondered Why The Stock Market Goes Up?*

**Formula on paper:** F8 (question).
**Why it fails:** "Have you ever wondered" is the second most-banned phrase on YouTube post-2025. The question itself is too generic — every viewer has wondered, the click promises nothing they can't get from a paragraph in any econ textbook.
**Fix:** Replace generic question with a specific puzzle. *Why Did The Stock Market Go Up The Day After Lehman Collapsed?* hits.

### Anti-pattern 8 — *I Built An App With Cursor And It's Amazing Honestly*

**Formula on paper:** F1 with first-person-anchor.
**Why it fails:** Adverbial closure ("amazing honestly") undercuts curiosity. The title resolves the question of how the app turned out before the click. Dev audience reads ad-hoc adverbs as influencer fluff.
**Fix:** Open the loop instead of closing it. *I Built A SaaS In 4 Hours With Cursor — Here's What Broke* hits.

---

## How the agent uses this companion

When generating titles for any video:

1. **Identify the niche** from the topic + channel context. Match to one of the 12 banks above (or fall back to the closest niche).
2. **Pull 5 closest-fit titles** from the bank as cite-able templates.
3. **Vary each through the topic** to produce 5 candidate titles per source.
4. **Cross-check candidates against the anti-pattern bank.** Reject any candidate that matches an anti-pattern.
5. **Rank candidates by predicted watch-time-per-impression** using the lift drivers from each source's annotation.
6. **Surface the top 6** to the user with the source-template citation visible (so the user understands why each was selected).

The agent does not generate titles in isolation. It pulls from the bank, varies through the topic, audits against anti-patterns, and ranks. This is faster, more consistent, and more outlier-aware than synthesizing from formulas alone.
